entries.title: Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference
entries.summary: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference now supports NVIDIA Dynamo for distributed inference, with multi-node and disaggregated serving, KV-aware routing, and automatic fault recovery. Serve large models across many nodes without building the orchestration layer yourself.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference

Serving large language models (LLMs) efficiently requires sufficient GPU memory and careful coordination of prompt processing and token generation. GLM-5.3’s FP8 weights, for example, exceed the 640 GB of GPU memory on a single 

ml.p5.48xlarge
instance, before accounting for KV cache and runtime overhead. Long prompts can also slow token generation when both share the same GPUs.

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference now supports NVIDIA Dynamo, combining Dynamo’s distributed inference capabilities with the infrastructure management of HyperPod to address these challenges. Dynamo is an open source distributed inference framework that supports multi-node deployment, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing with engines such as vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM. HyperPod supports these deployments with high-performance Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking, coordinated GPU scheduling, and node health monitoring and recovery. In this post, we illustrate multi-node and disaggregated serving through a deployment example, share benchmark results, and outline best practices for optimizing inference on HyperPod.

How the integration works

The HyperPod Inference add-on installs the Dynamo custom resource definitions and these serving and scheduling components:

  • HyperPod Inference Operator manages endpoint deployment through an InferenceEndpointConfig (IEC) custom resource. Its 
    dynamoSpec
    section supplies the Dynamo configuration.
  • Dynamo operator manages resources defined in a DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD), including the frontend, model workers, replica counts, and resource requirements.
  • Grove coordinates related groups of pods, including multi-node workers, and their scaling relationships.
  • Kubernetes AI (KAI) Scheduler places pods on GPU resources, using gang scheduling to schedule the pods required for a multi-node worker together.

AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) provide the Dynamo runtime, while the add-on manages integrated component versions. To adopt a supported Dynamo release, update the add-on.

Deployment architecture

The following diagram shows the deployment paths, serving components, and infrastructure management for disaggregated inference on SageMaker HyperPod. The Dynamo frontend routes requests to prefill workers, which process prompts, and decode workers, which generate tokens. These separate pools allow independent scaling and tuning. Both pools load the full model weights, and KV cache transfers between them over EFA.

Dynamo also supports aggregated serving, where prefill and decode run in the same worker. In either topology, workers can run on one instance or span multiple instances using tensor and pipeline parallelism. Dynamo’s KV-aware router considers reusable prefix KV cache and active worker load in both topologies. Prefix reuse can reduce prompt recomputation and improve time to first token, while load awareness helps avoid overloading workers. For more details on the Dynamo architecture, see the Dynamo Knowledge Base overview.

HyperPod provides node, GPU, and EFA health monitoring and manages node replacement, while the orchestration components recreate affected workers. Deployments configured through InferenceEndpointConfig with 

dynamoSpec
support invocation through SageMaker endpoints.

Two ways to configure your deployment

Whether you are new to HyperPod, new to Dynamo, or both, the add-on offers two deployment paths to fit your workflow:

Bring-your-own DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) lets existing Dynamo users continue using upstream documentation, recipes, and manifests, with the Dynamo operator managing the deployment. To bring an existing DGD to HyperPod, use a supported container image and configure storage, networking, and pod placement for your cluster.

InferenceEndpointConfig with dynamoSpec lets existing HyperPod Inference users deploy a new Dynamo endpoint using the same configuration format and OpenAI-compatible interface they already know. For the inference engine, you can choose vLLM, SGLang, or TensorRT-LLM, with vLLM used by default. The operator also supplies defaults for KV-aware routing and replica counts.

Both paths support single-instance and multi-node deployments. In either case, HyperPod manages node health and replacement. The table summarizes the responsibilities for each path.

Bring-your-own DGDInferenceEndpointConfig with dynamoSpec
You writeComplete DGD manifestIEC containing dynamoSpec
Best forTeams wanting direct control of the serving graph or reuse of existing DGDsTeams wanting managed endpoint setup through IEC
Model weightsYou configure downloading or mounting the weightsThe operator stages weights from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon FSx
Endpoint, TLS, registrationYou configure and manage these resourcesManaged through the HyperPod Inference Operator
AutoscalingYou configure and manage scalingKubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling (KEDA) through 
autoScalingSpec
for aggregated and disaggregated deployments

Deployment example: GLM-5.3

The following excerpts use the InferenceEndpointConfig (IEC) deployment path with vLLM on 

ml.p5.48xlarge
instances. Dynamo-specific settings belong under 
spec.dynamoSpec
. Model source and endpoint settings are included in the complete manifest.

Multi-node aggregated serving

This configuration runs one model-worker replica across two instances (16 GPUs), with two frontend replicas for request handling. Setting 

dynamoSpec.frontend.routingMode
to 
kv-aware
turns on KV-aware routing.

Here, 

spec.replicas
controls the number of model-worker replicas, while 
frontend.replicas
controls the number of frontend replicas.

Multi-node disaggregated serving

Replace 

aggregation
under 
spec.dynamoSpec
with the following 
disaggregation
block, keeping the preceding frontend configuration. Replica counts are set separately for prefill and decode. This example runs one prefill replica and two decode replicas, each spanning two instances, for a total of six instances.

Apply the deployment

Apply the complete manifest with 

kubectl apply
. The HyperPod Inference Operator makes the configured model weights available to the workers and generates the DGD. Grove and KAI Scheduler coordinate placement so that the pods required for each multi-node worker are scheduled together.

After the SageMaker endpoint is ready and configured for chat completions, clients can send an OpenAI-compatible request payload through the SageMaker Runtime API:

Benchmarks

We benchmarked Dynamo on SageMaker HyperPod across two models to compare serving configurations.

Disaggregated prefill and decode for Qwen3-235B

We used AIPerf to compare aggregated and disaggregated serving for 

Qwen3-235B-A22B-FP8
using Dynamo with TensorRT-LLM on two p5en.48xlarge instances (16 H200 GPUs). Requests contained 4,000 input tokens and 200 output tokens. We retained measured points that met two targets: P90 time to first token below one second, and median generation speed of at least 50 tokens per second per user. Among these points, disaggregated serving achieved 2.05× the highest aggregated throughput: 207 versus 101 output tokens per second per GPU, at concurrency 80 and 32, respectively.

Multi-node aggregated serving for Qwen3.5-397B

Dynamo supports multi-node serving in both aggregated and disaggregated modes for models that exceed a single instance’s GPU memory. To evaluate a worker spanning nodes, we used AIPerf to benchmark multi-node aggregated serving for Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 with Dynamo and vLLM, using TP4 × PP2 and eight active H200 GPUs. This model fits on one instance, so in practice you would not split it. It serves here as a controlled baseline. We compared eight GPUs on one p5en.48xlarge against four GPUs on each of two instances, using the same model, parallelism, and workload configuration. With an agentic workload featuring high prefix reuse at concurrency 32, the two-node configuration delivered 126.4 output tokens per second per GPU, retaining 99.1 percent of single-node throughput. This shows that Dynamo on SageMaker HyperPod can serve a model that needs more than one instance across nodes. The node boundary itself does not become a significant throughput penalty.

Best practices for optimized inference

NVIDIA Dynamo provides recipes and tools to help you select a serving configuration, benchmark performance, and tune your deployment on SageMaker HyperPod.

  • Start with a matching recipe – Choose a Dynamo recipe for your model, inference engine, and GPU type. Account for model weights, KV cache, and runtime memory when sizing workers. For supported configurations, AISimulate can help compare aggregated and disaggregated serving, choose parallelism, and size prefill and decode worker pools before testing on GPUs.
  • Verify communication before benchmarking – For deployments spanning instances, confirm that communication uses the intended EFA transport, including KV-cache transfers between prefill and decode workers. See the Dynamo EFA guide.
  • Benchmark representative traffic – Replay your traffic with AIPerf, or use a generated agentic trace with representative prompt lengths, output lengths, and prefix reuse. Sweep concurrency for each configuration, retain points meeting your SLAs, and choose based on cost and latency priorities.
  • Tune from measured bottlenecks – Adjust topology and worker allocation before engine settings, changing one variable at a time. Follow the performance tuning guide, or use Dynamo optimization agent skills to assist with benchmarking and tuning. Validate each candidate on your target HyperPod deployment.

Conclusion

NVIDIA Dynamo on SageMaker HyperPod Inference simplifies deploying and operating large models with multi-node serving, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing. The managed add-on installs the serving components, and configuration defaults simplify endpoint setup. HyperPod manages model weights, auto-scales clusters based on GPU and inference metrics, monitors node health, and replaces failed nodes. Together, these capabilities reduce undifferentiated infrastructure work so teams can focus on their models and applications. Get started with the setup instructions and complete deployment examples in the linked repository.

Acknowledgements

The authors would like to thank Eliuth Triana, Felipe Garcia, Sanjana Checker, Junyuan Yang, Jiahong Liu, Anish Maddipoti, Jacob Kern and Abdullahi Olaoye from NVIDIA for their contributions to this post. We also would like to thank Can Sun, Ophelia Yang, Aryaman Kothari, David Oh, and Ayush Kumar from AWS for their contributions.

entries.title: Reducing token costs and latency in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore JSON workloads
entries.summary: As production agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore process multi-megabyte JSON payloads, token costs and latency climb. This post shares three composable strategies: offloading heavy artifacts to Amazon S3, on-demand result paging, and dictionary compaction. Together they cut per-turn token use by up to 71% and latency by up to 80%.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Reducing token costs and latency in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore JSON workloads

As enterprises build production agents with dozens of tools and large structured inputs, token consumption and latency become the primary blockers to a good user experience. When these agents process large JSON data, every additional tool invocation injects the full payload into the large language model (LLM) context window, causing token usage and response latency to spike. Over multi-turn conversations, this pressure compounds, driving up costs and degrading response quality. Effectively managing context-window pressure in agentic systems is key to reliability and responsiveness at scale. In this post, we share three composable strategies we used to build a production agent for Flightscape that handles 20 MB+ JSON payloads. You can apply them to reduce token costs, lower latency, and maintain full reasoning capability across extended sessions. Together, these optimizations reduced token consumption by up to 71% and cut average latency by up to 80% across our benchmark runs on a representative 23 MB payload.

Solution overview

Flightscape is an airline operations platform that helps airlines plan and manage their crews, flights, and operations. As part of Flightscape’s crew management capabilities, we built a Training Schedule Optimization agent that verifies crew training schedule assignments against business rules. With 40+ tools and JSON inputs in megabytes, this agent could answer complex queries across crew assignments, scheduling, and resource allocation. Although the agent delivered the required functionality, average request latencies exceeded 15 seconds across most calls. Every tool call injected its full payload into the model context, inflating token counts and costs. On larger datasets, the context window filled up before the agent could finish reasoning. The following diagram (Figure 1) details the agentic architecture and data flow:

In Figure 1, the Optimizer receives a Request JSON and produces a Response JSON, which is then validated by a Business Rules Validator to generate a Validation Report JSON. All three JSON documents are ingested by an AI Agent that provides a conversational interface for users to query optimization results, understand validation errors, and explore scheduling assignments. The agent is built with LangGraph, an open source framework by LangChain, and runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can be applied to validate and filter the agent’s conversational responses, helping facilitate responsible AI practices in production deployments. We defined a custom agent state that holds the data needed by our tools: optimization request JSON, optimization response JSON, and validation report JSON. We also added basic statistics and cache data to state for rich queries. The agent uses an Amazon Bedrock model for reasoning and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to persist chat interactions across turns, and each turn follows this flow (Figure 2):

This is what the state structure looks like. The state references TOPT (Training Optimizer) request and response objects, which represent the crew scheduling inputs and optimization results:

Note: This state originally held heavy payloads inline. Later sections explain how we moved large artifacts out of conversational context to reduce token usage.

We implemented three strategies to reduce the token costs, latency, and memory overhead caused by passing large JSON payloads through the model context. The following diagram (Figure 3) shows how the three strategies fit into a single agent turn. Strategy 1 runs at the start and end of each turn, and Strategies 2 and 3 run each time a tool returns a result.

At the start of a turn, the 

hydrate_state()
function restores lightweight session state from AgentCore memory. When a tool returns an oversized list or dictionary, the agent stores the full result in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and passes the model a compact summary with a handle. The model can then retrieve more detail with 
get_result_page_tool()
. At the end of the turn, the 
dehydrate_state()
function writes heavy payloads to the 
S3ArtifactStore
and saves only references to AgentCore memory. The following sections describe each strategy in detail.

Prerequisites

To implement these strategies, make sure the following are in place:

  • An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock and a supported model.
  • An Amazon S3 bucket for artifact storage.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory enabled for session-state persistence.
  • A LangGraph-based agent (or equivalent graph-orchestration framework) with tool-calling support.
  • A Python 3.12+ environment with 
    boto3
    , 
    langchain-core
    , and 
    langgraph
    .

Optimization strategies

The companion code is available in this GitHub repository.

Strategy 1: Persist lightweight session state, offload heavy artifacts

Our first optimization was to change how we persist session state. Initially, large payloads were being stored too close to the conversational state. We therefore moved heavy artifacts (request JSON, response JSON, validation data, and other large derived payloads) to Amazon S3. AgentCore memory then persists only stable references to these objects, keeping the session state lightweight.

To support this, we introduced a dedicated persisted-state schema that keeps only lightweight fields and artifact references. The live graph state still includes parsed domain objects for tool execution, but persistence now writes a dehydrated form. At runtime, tools hydrate heavy payloads on demand using those references, instead of loading everything on every turn.

This 

PersistedState
schema is what gets written to AgentCore Memory:

The updated 

GraphState
mirrors these references alongside the live domain objects:

The 

dehydrate_state
function strips heavy payloads from the live state and returns the lightweight persisted form along with the artifacts to upload:

Rehydration reverses this process. When a session resumes, we rebuild the live graph state: deserialize LangChain messages, re-parse raw payloads into domain objects, and restore every reference key so later turns can locate their artifacts:

Both dehydration and rehydration rely on the artifact store returning a consistent reference for each payload. Instead of minting a random key, we derive the reference from the payload itself. This approach, known as content addressing, serializes the JSON with sorted keys and compact separators, and uses the SHA-256 digest of those bytes as the reference.

The 

_content_hash
helper produces a deterministic SHA-256 reference from a JSON-serializable payload:

Content addressing makes writes idempotent. Identical payloads map to the same key, so a turn that re-serializes an unchanged request JSON reuses the object already in the bucket instead of uploading it again. The S3-backed store exposes a 

put_json
and 
get_json
interface. It also keeps a small in-process cache, so payloads already read or written during the current invocation do not require a second S3 round trip.

The 

S3ArtifactStore
class wraps the 
put_json
/
get_json
interface with an in-process cache and content-addressed keys:

Offloading heavy artifacts to S3 and persisting only lightweight references reduced per-turn latency and the volume of data stored in AgentCore memory. With heavy payloads no longer persisted inline, tool-call responses became the dominant consumer of context tokens, prompting us to introduce result paging.

Strategy 2: Page large result lists on demand

Even after moving heavy payload persistence to Amazon S3, we still had a major token bottleneck at tool-response time. Many tool results were too large, which created two problems. First, we were sending full lists to the model even when it only needed a small subset, making each turn slower and more expensive. Second, those full list payloads were injected into context, which quickly consumed the context window over multi-turn conversations.

In some cases, a single tool response exceeded 80,000 tokens, and the cost compounded as users continued interacting with the agent. We wanted to preserve full data access without sending everything by default. To solve this, we introduced on-demand result paging for large tool outputs. Instead of returning full lists, tools now return a compact payload with total count, a small sample, and a result handle.

When a tool result exceeds the sample-size threshold, the full list is stored in S3 and only a compact summary is returned to the model:

The handle points to the complete result stored in S3. When the agent needs more detail, it calls a paging tool with the handle and requests only the required slice, for example using offset and limit.

The 

get_result_page_tool
function lets the model retrieve additional slices of a stored result by handle, offset, and limit:

On-demand paging kept the full list in S3 and served only the requested slice per turn, controlling context growth and significantly reducing token usage. However, not all oversized outputs were lists. Some tools returned large dictionaries that required a different compaction approach.

Strategy 3: Compact oversized dictionary outputs

Unlike lists, dictionary outputs contain deeply nested structured data that are useful for reasoning but typically too expensive to include verbatim on each turn. We needed a compact representation that preserved structural cues while drastically cutting the token footprint.

To solve this, we introduced descriptor-based compaction for oversized dictionary outputs. Instead of returning an oversized dictionary in full, we return a compact descriptor:

  • List fields are represented by count and sample.
  • Nested dictionaries are summarized by key count.
  • Scalar values remain inline where useful.

The full payload is stored in the artifact store, and the response includes a result handle. When the agent needs deeper detail, it uses that handle to fetch only the required data. This response format remained navigable for the model while significantly reducing unnecessary token usage.

The 

_oversized_descriptor
function builds a compact structural summary of a dictionary payload, preserving field types and sample data without the full content:

If the serialized output still exceeds the character limit, the fallback stores the full payload and replaces the response with its descriptor:

With lightweight persisted state, on-demand paging, and dictionary compaction in place, token growth became predictable and the agent stayed responsive even on multi-megabyte datasets.

Results

To validate the impact of these three strategies, we ran the same set of questions over the same dataset against both the pre-optimization and optimized versions of the agent. We then compared token usage and latency in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability (a capability of AgentCore), and observed clear improvements in both cost and responsiveness.

Across a 5-question conversation run, total token usage dropped by approximately 71%, from ~289,500 to ~82,900 tokens, while average trace latency decreased by nearly 80%, from 15.4 s to 3.1 s (Figure 4). Across 100 sample questions (Figure 5), total tokens fell from 23.6 M to 8.5 M (64%) and average trace latency dropped from 7,930 ms to 2,461 ms (69%).

The effect was most dramatic on large single-turn payloads. Table 1 breaks down the per-turn impact for the heaviest single query (listing valid crews across every validation category).

MetricBeforeAfterReduction
Input tokens~32,000~8,00075%
Output tokens~2,80047783%
Turn latency~165 s9.9 s94%

Table 1: Input, output, and latency impact

Figure 6 and Figure 7 show the corresponding trace details before and after optimization.

These gains came primarily from avoiding full payload injection into model context at every turn. Instead, the model now receives compact summaries first and fetches additional detail only when needed.

The improvement was also visible in the trace timelines: the pre-optimization turn stretched to nearly 2 minutes 46 seconds, while the optimized turn completed in about 15 seconds (Figure 9).

The changes also improved behavior in longer conversations. Context growth became more predictable across turns, and the agent remained responsive even when users asked follow-up questions over large datasets. In practice, this shifted the system from compounding token cost to a more controlled, demand-driven access pattern.

Most importantly, these gains came without sacrificing capability. Full payloads remain in artifact storage and can be retrieved through handles whenever deeper inspection is needed. At Flightscape, this pattern provides a foundation for bringing conversational AI capabilities to complex airline operations workflows, keeping the underlying AI experience scalable and cost efficient.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources you created for this walkthrough:

  • Empty and optionally delete the S3 bucket used for the artifact store, or remove all objects under the artifact prefix (for example, artifacts/).
  • Delete any Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agents and associated AgentCore memory sessions created during testing.
  • Remove AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles and policies created for S3 or Bedrock access.
  • Delete Amazon CloudWatch log groups generated by the agent runtime.
  • Remove any Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) endpoints or networking resources provisioned for this walkthrough.

Conclusion

If your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent handles large JSON data, start by identifying which tool outputs dominate your context window. Begin with offloading artifacts to S3 (Strategy 1) because it provides the foundation for the other optimizations, then add paging (Strategy 2) and compaction (Strategy 3) as needed to improve the token usage and latency of your agents. To get started, clone the GitHub repository and adapt the strategies to your own agent. To learn more about building agents with AgentCore and LangGraph, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation and the LangGraph framework documentation.

entries.title: Cut generative AI costs: Code for rules, models for judgment
entries.summary: The biggest cost lever in a generative AI system is whether you call a model at all. Learn how to decide whether each workflow step needs a model, and map each option to AWS: deterministic code, a constrained decision call, or a right-sized model on Amazon Bedrock.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Cut generative AI costs: Code for rules, models for judgment

The biggest cost lever in a generative AI system is whether you call a model at all. We often see teams route every task through a large language model (LLM), including input validation, formatting, and routing. Each call is cheap in isolation, but at production scale these small costs become one of the largest line items in the architecture. Wherever a deterministic rule can do the job, skipping the model saves money, cuts latency, and removes a source of non-determinism. In this post, you learn how to decide whether each step in a workflow needs a model at all. You can then map each option to AWS: deterministic code, a constrained decision call, or a right-sized model on Amazon Bedrock.

Why unneeded model calls add up

The pattern usually starts in a prototype. A model call works for one step, so it becomes the default for the next. Those steps include validating input, reformatting a request body, and picking a route. At prototype volume, nobody notices the cost.

At production volume, unneeded model calls cost you in three ways:

  • Spend grows with request count, even for low-value steps.
  • Latency stacks, because every model call in a chain adds hundreds of milliseconds.
  • Output can vary, because the same input can return a different answer. That makes testing harder and audits slower.

Each new model launch then restarts the debate about which model to use. The earlier question, whether the step needs a model at all, goes unasked.

Cost guidance, including the AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens, often starts at model selection. This post starts one step earlier: Does the step need a model at all?

How to decide whether a step needs a model

Figure 1 shows the whole decision as a flowchart with three labeled lanes: Runs as code, Questions, and Runs on a model. Take each workflow step through three questions in order, and stop at the first option that meets the step’s requirements:

  • Can a rule check success, such as a format, a schema, a keyword, or a range? If a rule settles only part of the step, a fast path runs the rule first.
  • Can a model write the rule once, such as a regular expression or a JSON schema?
  • Does the step pick one answer from a fixed list, such as a route, a class, or yes or no?

If the answer to all three is no, the step is open-ended and runs on a right-sized model.

Consider a customer support assistant. The following table shows how five of its steps go through the chart.

#StepPath through the chartWhere it runs
1Check an order number’s formatA rule can check success.Amazon API Gateway REST API request validation, or an AWS Lambda function
2Route a message by intentA rule settles part of it. A keyword match on the fast path resolves messages such as “refund”, and the residual goes to the third question.An AWS Step Functions Choice state that uses JSONata. The residual goes to a constrained decision call.
3Extract a tracking number from a carrier emailA model can write the rule once. It drafts a regular expression, and you review and commit it.Code, as a committed pattern in AWS Lambda
4Pick one of four support queues for a ticketThe answer comes from a fixed list.A constrained decision call. Unsure answers escalate to the right-sized model.
5Draft a reply to the customerThe task is open-ended.The right-sized model, the smallest Amazon Bedrock model that meets the requirements

You can use a model when a task is open-ended, ambiguous, or generative: summarizing a document, drafting a reply, extracting meaning from prose. Use deterministic code when the task has a checkable rule: an email format, a schema, an exact keyword, a numeric range. The following table shows what you trade away when you send a rule-shaped task to a model.

PropertyDeterministic codeModel call
Cost per invocationTypically orders of magnitude lowerPer-token, non-trivial at scale
LatencySingle-digit milliseconds or lessHundreds of milliseconds
Correctness on a well-specified ruleExact for the rule as writtenHigh, but with a non-zero error rate
AuditabilityThe rule sits in source controlHarder to explain to an auditor
Behavior over timeStable until you change itChanges when you move to a new model version, or when a version is retired

A model can also hallucinate and return different answers to the same input. A temperature of 0 makes varied answers less likely, but it doesn’t guarantee identical output. Amazon Bedrock model evaluation and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails help you measure and contain these risks. A rule has neither problem, which is one reason regulated workloads favor rules. A useful test: If you can write the acceptance test as a rule, you can usually write the step as a rule. For more information, refer to Orchestration models: From rule-based to AI-native in AWS Prescriptive Guidance.

Decide, don’t generate

Most routing and classification steps sit between a rule and open-ended generation. A rule can’t decide every case, but these steps don’t need generated text either. They need one answer from a fixed list of options that you define in advance, like the support queues in the preceding example. Use a component that limits its output to the allowed answers and gives you a signal for when to escalate. Confident answers proceed, and uncertain ones escalate. The AWS Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens describes this tiered, confidence-based escalation. On AWS, you can build it four ways:

  • A small Amazon Bedrock model with structured outputs – The answer is limited to an 
    enum
    of options, plus an ‘unsure’ option that triggers escalation. This is the model’s own judgment, not a calibrated score, so check it against labeled data before you use it to decide escalation.
  • Embedding similarity – Embed the input with an Amazon Bedrock embeddings model and pick the nearest labeled example. Use the similarity score as an escalation signal, and set its threshold on labeled data.
  • Strands Decider, an experimental open source decision model under the Apache License 2.0 – It picks from options or scores against a rubric, and it returns a calibrated confidence with each answer. Its README reports that answers at a confidence of 0.9 or more are right about 95 percent of the time on short classification tasks. Because the model is experimental, validate that result on your own data before you use it in production. You host it yourself, for example on an Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint, by following the deployment guides in its repository.
  • A trained classifier on Amazon SageMaker AI – It returns class probabilities with low latency and cost once you have labeled training data.

The following JSON schema limits a structured-output answer to four queues plus ‘unsure’. Amazon Bedrock requires every object in the schema to set 

additionalProperties
to 
false
.

Whichever option you choose, check its escalation signal against your own labeled data, and set any threshold there. Keep your authorization decisions, such as a refund limit, in a rule.

The deterministic fast-path pattern

Many cost patterns focus on routing between models. The fast path goes one level earlier: Run the deterministic check first, and send only what the rule can’t settle to a model. Intent routing is one example. Many messages carry an unambiguous signal, such as “refund” or “reset my password”, which a keyword match resolves in single-digit milliseconds or less. If rules resolve 95 percent of requests, only 1 in 20 requests reaches a model, before any savings from model selection. (Illustrative arithmetic, not a benchmark.)

On AWS, you compose this from existing building blocks:

  • AWS Step Functions Choice states branch before the workflow invokes any model.
  • AWS Lambda hosts rules that need more than a Choice state, such as validation and schema checks.
  • Amazon API Gateway (REST API) request validation rejects malformed input before any compute runs.
  • A constrained decision call or an Amazon Bedrock model handles only the residual.

The following Choice state is a keyword fast path. It uses JSONata to send refund and password-reset messages straight to code, and it sends everything else to the constrained decision call.

You can also let a model write the rule once instead of running it every time. Have it draft a regular expression or a JSON schema, review it, and commit it. At runtime the rule runs at rule speed and cost. Review a model-written regular expression, and test it against known good and bad inputs. Avoid nested quantifiers such as 

(a+)+
, which can make matching very slow on some inputs (regular expression denial of service, or ReDoS).

When you do generate, Amazon Bedrock structured outputs constrain a response to a JSON schema that you define. The response then matches the schema, so your code can parse it without custom parsing logic (check content for correctness). Keep range checks, such as numeric bounds and length limits, in code. For supported models and schema features, refer to Get validated JSON results from models.

If your rules live in configuration, allow only known primitives, such as regular expressions, schema checks, keyword lists, and range checks. Never run arbitrary code from a configuration file.

When you do need a model, right-size it

Choose the cheapest and fastest model that meets your quality floor. That is often not the newest or largest model. The Generative AI Lens covers this in its best practice on right-sizing model selection. Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock covers it in depth. Define the requirements before you compare models:

  • Quality floor: The minimum acceptable output quality, measured on a golden evaluation set (labeled examples of the task with known-correct answers).
  • Cost ceiling: The most you pay per request or per successful outcome.
  • Latency target: The p95 or p99 response time the experience can tolerate.
  • Compliance constraints: Requirements such as data residency that can rule out candidates.

Amazon Bedrock offers many model families and sizes behind one API, so you can right-size each task without changing your integration. Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing routes each request to a suitable model within a supported model family. Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation transfers knowledge from a larger model to a smaller, cheaper one for your use case. Model providers evaluate a new frontier model on broad benchmarks, but your workload is one task with one quality floor. A larger model can add cost and latency without improving that task. Before you switch, evaluate each launch against your requirements, such as quality on your golden evaluation set and your latency target.

Treat model choice as tested configuration

The Generative AI Lens recommends testing candidate models against your ground truth data and having a way to update the model quickly. Go further and treat the decision as a tested configuration:

  • Keep a golden evaluation set per task, with labeled ground truth, and run it in continuous integration.
  • Gate on your requirements. Treat a cheaper model that drops below the quality floor as a regression.
  • Put the model behind a configuration flag so that you can reverse a swap.
  • Verify with the right oracle. Check rules against ground truth. Reserve model-as-judge evaluation for open-ended outputs.
  • Watch for drift. Sample some rule-resolved requests through a model in shadow mode, and reclassify a step when they disagree.

Putting it into practice

Spend model capacity where judgment is needed, and nowhere else. You can get there in four steps:

  • Instrument – Tag every call as deterministic code, a constrained decision call, or a model call. Track cost per successful outcome.
  • Move the rules to code – Run rule-checkable steps on AWS Lambda or AWS Step Functions. This is usually the largest and safest win.
  • Add constrained decision calls – Route fixed-choice steps through a call that escalates when it is unsure.
  • Test before you switch models – Run every new model through your golden evaluation set before it becomes the default.

Conclusion

In this post, you learned how to decide whether a workflow step needs a model at all. Rules belong in deterministic code, and fixed choices belong in a constrained decision call. Open-ended work goes to a right-sized Amazon Bedrock model. Aim to meet each requirement at the lowest cost and latency that your quality floor allows. Ask whether a step needs a model before you ask which one.

For more information, refer to these posts on the AWS Artificial Intelligence Blog:

  • Use decision models with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations.
  • Use Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing for cost and latency benefits.
  • Structured outputs on Amazon Bedrock: Schema-compliant AI responses.
  • Fix evaluation bias to unlock better models on Amazon Bedrock.

To try a constrained decision call, open the Amazon Bedrock console, or deploy Strands Decider from its GitHub repository.

Start with one high-volume workflow and measure how much of it never needed a model.

entries.title: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing
entries.summary: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache-aware routing, a new strategy that routes each request to the instance holding the longest cached match for its prompt. Learn how it works, when to use it compared with prefix-aware routing, and how to enable, invoke, and verify it on single model and inference component endpoints.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing

Today, Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing (KV-aware routing), a new routing strategy for real-time endpoints. It uses the cache state that the model container reports. It sends each request to an instance that already holds a long cached match for its prompt and isn’t too busy. It’s for teams that serve large language models (LLMs) with multi-turn conversations, long shared prompts, or heavy load. You turn it on in two places: add one environment variable to your model so the container reports its cache contents, and set 

RoutingStrategy
to 
KV_AWARE
in the endpoint configuration. Your clients call the endpoint with the same APIs as before.

Here’s the problem it solves: LLM applications such as chat assistants, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), and agents with long system prompts send many requests that start with the same text. A model keeps the work it did on a prompt in GPU memory, the KV cache, and skips that work when the same start reaches the same instance again. In part 1 of this series, we introduced prefix-aware routing for Amazon SageMaker AI, which sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. Prefix-aware routing infers where a prefix is cached from the request alone, so it can’t tell when an instance has evicted that cache.

Prefix-aware routing picks an instance from the request alone. It hashes the start of the request, up to the 

PrefixLength
you configure (bytes of the 
InvokeEndpoint
payload, or characters of the message text for the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API), and sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. It never sees what an instance actually has cached. This works well when every request starts with the same shared text, and less well in two cases:

The cache on an instance changes over time. An instance evicts older KV cache entries when its GPU memory fills up, but the router keeps sending matching requests there as if the cache were still warm.

A conversation starts out short. In a multi-turn chat, each turn adds to the history. While the request is still shorter than 

PrefixLength
, every new turn changes the text the router hashes, so the next turn can land on a different instance than the one that cached the earlier turns. The turns of a conversation stay on one instance only after the request grows past 
PrefixLength
.

In this post, we explain how KV-aware routing works, when to use it, and how to enable, invoke, and verify it on single model endpoints and inference component endpoints.

How KV-aware routing works

KV-aware routing has three parts: the model container reports what it has cached, SageMaker AI keeps a managed cache index of that state for the endpoint, and the endpoint uses the index to choose an instance for each request.

When you turn events on with 

SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG
, the container publishes a KV cache event each time it stores or evicts cache entries, and SageMaker AI uses these events to keep the index current. The index holds only pointers: one-way, truncated hashes of cached content, each mapped to the instance or inference component copy that holds it. It never stores prompts, token IDs, request payloads, or KV tensors. When a request arrives, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks up the tokens in the index. The index returns the instances or inference component copies that hold part of the prompt in their cache, and how much of it each one holds. For example, if instance A holds the cached start of a conversation, the next turn of that conversation goes to A. Because the index matches on tokens rather than a fixed number of bytes, a multi-turn history can match in full as it grows. A request that shares only part of its prompt still goes to the instance with the longest match.

The endpoint then picks among these candidates by weighing how much of the prompt each one has cached against how busy it is. A candidate that is too busy is skipped, so if the instance with the longest match is busy, the request goes to the next-best one that is available. If no candidate has a useful match or all of them are busy, the request falls back to load-aware routing, as described in Routing overhead and fallbacks. You don’t configure a concurrency threshold for this, as you do with prefix-aware routing. The index also follows the fleet. When you scale in, entries for removed instances are dropped. When you scale out or an update replaces instances, the new instances start with empty caches, so latency can be higher for a short time.

In Figure 1, the endpoint has three instances, A, B, and C. Each instance runs the same model in its own model container (the AWS vLLM Deep Learning Container listed in Requirements and limits) and has its own KV cache in GPU memory, so each instance holds different cached content: A holds turns 1 to 3 of conversation 1, B holds conversations 2 and 3, and C holds document 7. When turn 4 of conversation 1 arrives (step 1), the router tokenizes it and looks it up in the managed cache index (step 2). The index shows that A holds the first 6,000 of the request’s 6,200 tokens, so the router sends the request to A (step 3), and A only has to compute the remaining tokens. If A is busy, the router sends the request to the least busy instance instead (step 4). KV-aware routing needs a choice of destinations, so it is active only with at least two instances, or at least two copies of an inference component. With a single instance, every request goes to that instance and the setting has no effect.

Routing strategies on SageMaker AI

With this launch, SageMaker AI offers four routing strategies for real-time endpoints. You set the strategy per production variant in the 

RoutingConfig
of your endpoint configuration.
StrategyHow it routesRecommended for
RANDOM (default)Sends each request to a randomly chosen instance.General-purpose workloads, non-LLM models, and requests that are interchangeable.
LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTSSends each request to the instance with the fewest in-flight requests.Workloads where processing time varies and you want to keep all instances equally busy.
PREFIX_AWARESends requests that share the same prompt prefix, up to PrefixLength, to the same instance. Overflows to another instance at ConcurrencyThreshold.LLM workloads with shared text at a fixed position at the start of the request, on any serving framework that supports prefix caching.
KV_AWARE (new)Sends each request to an instance that holds a matching cached prefix, based on cache state reported by the container, weighing match length against load. Falls back to load-aware routing.LLM workloads on a supported container with multi-turn conversations, frequent cache eviction, or requests that share only part of their start.

Prefix-aware or KV-aware

Both strategies send requests to where their prefix is likely to be cached. They differ in how they know where that is, and in what they need from your container.

Prefix-aware routingKV-aware routing
Source of cache locationInferred from the request prefixCache state reported by the container
Added latency per request1.3–1.9 milliseconds in part 1A few milliseconds for short prompts, more for long ones, mostly for tokenization
MatchingFirst PrefixLength bytes (Invoke API) or characters (OpenAI-compatible API)Tokens, longest cached match
ParametersPrefixLength, ConcurrencyThresholdNone needed
ContainerAny container with prefix caching onA supported container, with prefix caching and KV cache events on (see Requirements and limits)
Request payloadAnyOpenAI-compatible Completions or Chat Completions format

Performance

We measured KV-aware routing against random routing in two ways: a large-scale benchmark on production-sized instances, and a smaller, reproducible comparison you can follow in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.

Benchmark results

In our benchmarks with Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on seven 

ml.p5.48xlarge
instances, we ran 30-minute tests with 20 or 100 simulated users holding multi-turn chats and document Q&A sessions, with prompts of up to about 64,000 tokens. Compared with random routing, and with long prompts under load, KV-aware routing reduced p50 time to first token (TTFT) by up to 97 percent and increased throughput by up to 234 percent. It raised the KV cache hit rate from 3–48 percent to 80–93 percent. Long prompts gained even at lower load. The gain was smallest with short prompts, where there is less prefill to save. Results depend on your workload. To measure them for your own traffic, use the checks in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.

Routing overhead and fallbacks

Before it routes a request, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks it up in the managed cache index. The lookup takes a few milliseconds for short prompts and longer for long ones, mostly for tokenization, but it stays small next to the time a cache hit saves. For text-only requests that use standard options, the tokens it computes are passed to the model, so the prompt isn’t tokenized twice.

If the lookup is slow, finds no useful match, or all matching instances are busy, the endpoint routes the request with load-aware routing, the same behavior as the 

LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS
strategy. The request is still served, without the cache benefit. The same happens when the endpoint can’t tokenize a request, except in the two error cases described in Invoking the endpoint. These fallbacks aren’t reported in the SageMaker AI console or metrics at launch, so use the checks in Verify that KV-aware routing is working to confirm that routing is effective for your traffic.

With very short prompts there is less prefill to save, so prefix-aware routing can be all you need.

When to use KV-aware routing

Prefix-aware routing needs no changes to your container, but it can’t see what an instance actually holds. KV-aware routing asks the container what it holds, which makes it more precise. It pays off when there is a lot of cached context to reuse and that cache is under pressure: long prompts, high load, and instances that run short of GPU memory for the KV cache. When that happens, the container evicts the least recently used parts of the cache, including parts of shared prompts and conversation history.

For example, a support assistant runs on three instances, and each conversation begins with the same 6,000-token knowledge-base excerpt. Conversation 1 starts on instance A, which caches the excerpt. Traffic rises, A runs short of memory, and the container evicts most of that excerpt. Instance B recently served another conversation over the same excerpt and still holds its first 4,000 tokens. When the next turn of conversation 1 arrives, prefix-aware routing sends it to A again, and A recomputes the excerpt. With KV-aware routing, A’s container has already reported the eviction, so the index shows that B holds the longest match, and the request goes to B, which recomputes only the remaining tokens. At low load, A wouldn’t have evicted anything, and both strategies would have sent the request to A with the cache intact.

KV-aware routing helps most when requests reuse cached context in ways a fixed-length prefix can’t capture:

Multi-turn conversations: Each turn sends the full conversation history, so the cached prefix grows with every turn. KV-aware routing matches the whole cached history and keeps each conversation on the instance that holds it. This matters most for long conversations. After the managed cache index reflects an eviction, the router doesn’t keep sending the conversation to an instance that has already dropped its cache.

High-throughput inference with shared context: RAG applications prepend retrieved documents, and assistants send long system prompts with every request. KV-aware routing fits when these prompts are long and instances are under memory pressure. With a stable shared prefix and moderate load, prefix-aware routing also fits. Put the shared content first and in the same order: if the same documents appear in a different order, the prompts no longer share a start, so they don’t match.

Workloads where prefix length is hard to tune: With prefix-aware routing, you choose a 

PrefixLength
that covers your shared text without scattering requests that should stay together. KV-aware routing has no prefix length to tune, because it matches on what is actually cached.

Prefix-aware routing is a good fit, with no container changes, if your requests share a stable system prompt or document at the start, your prompts are short, or load is moderate. In these cases, instances have enough GPU memory to keep the shared text cached, so both strategies find it. Prefix-aware routing is also the choice if your container isn’t supported by KV-aware routing, because it works with any container that has prefix caching turned on. If your requests are short and interchangeable, or your model isn’t an LLM, there is little cached context to reuse, so use 

RANDOM
or 
LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS
.

If you aren’t sure which fits, start with prefix-aware routing, run your own traffic against a 

KV_AWARE
endpoint, and compare time to first token, throughput, and hit rate as described in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.

Requirements and limits

Before you enable KV-aware routing, check that your container, endpoint, and requests meet these requirements:

Container: At launch, KV-aware routing supports the AWS vLLM Deep Learning Container for SageMaker AI: images with vLLM 0.33.0 or later, or the Amazon Linux build 

server-sagemaker-cuda-v2.8.0
or later. Prefix caching must be on, which is the default, and KV cache events must be turned on with the 
SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG
environment variable, as shown in How to enable it. SageMaker AI doesn’t set it for you.

Endpoints and instances: Real-time single model endpoints and inference component endpoints, including dynamic Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters, on GPU instance types. You can also configure KV-aware routing with AWS CloudFormation. Routing is active only with at least two instances for a single model endpoint, or at least two copies of an inference component, which can be on the same instance. With fewer, you can still set 

KV_AWARE
and the endpoint isn’t rejected, but every request goes to the single instance or copy.

Requests: OpenAI-compatible Completions or Chat Completions payloads, sent with 

InvokeEndpoint
, 
InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream
, or the SageMaker AI OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. 
InvokeEndpointWithBidirectionalStream
isn’t supported. If you set the 
model
field, it must match the value of 
SM_VLLM_MODEL
.

SDK versions: Detailed observability, which you use to track the KV cache hit rate, needs AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) version 2.35.6 or later, or Boto3 version 1.43.31 or later.

SageMaker AI checks these requirements before your endpoint serves traffic. If a check fails, the request or deployment fails with a message that describes what is missing. For the full list of settings, validation behavior, and quotas, see the SageMaker AI documentation.

How to enable it

You turn on KV-aware routing in two places: the model and the endpoint configuration. The example notebook runs every step end to end, for both a single model endpoint and an inference component endpoint.

1. Turn on KV cache events in the model – When you create the model, add 

SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG
to the container environment. Without it, the endpoint has no cache state to route on. The ports in this setting are used only inside the instance, so you don’t open them to your network.

2. Choose KV-aware routing in the endpoint configuration – Set 

RoutingStrategy
to 
KV_AWARE
in the 
RoutingConfig
of the production variant:

If your container image is built for CUDA 13, also set 

InferenceAmiVersion
in the production variant to an AMI that supports it, such as 
al2023-ami-sagemaker-inference-gpu-4-1
. Otherwise the container can fail to start. See Inference GPU drivers.

Check that your account has enough endpoint quota for the instance type and count you choose, and request an increase in Service Quotas if needed.

The same 

RoutingConfig
setting works for inference component endpoints, including dynamic LoRA adapters. For adapters, KV-aware routing chooses among the instances that already have the adapter loaded.

Invoking the endpoint

Nothing changes in how you call the endpoint. Send a Chat Completions payload with 

InvokeEndpoint
, or with 
InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream
and 
"stream": true
in the request body:

You can also call the endpoint with the OpenAI Python client through the SageMaker AI OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. The Use the OpenAI-compatible API with SageMaker AI notebook on GitHub shows how, for both single model endpoints and inference components.

KV-aware routing doesn’t apply the multi-tenant prefix isolation from part 1: it ignores the prefix-aware ID header and the 

prompt_cache_key
field. A request that sets a top-level 
cache_salt
field to a non-null value is rejected with a 400 error.

KV-aware routing adds two error cases: a request whose 

model
field names a model that the container doesn’t serve fails with a 
ModelError
, and a request with a non-null 
cache_salt
is rejected with a 400 error. Errors from inference itself are returned as before, and your model container’s own logs in Amazon CloudWatch can help you find the cause. The endpoint doesn’t deliver logs about its KV-aware routing decisions to your account, so use the checks in Verify that KV-aware routing is working, such as 
cached_tokens
per request and the KV cache hit rate, to see how routing behaves.

Verify that KV-aware routing is working

KV-aware routing doesn’t add metrics of its own, so you check its effect on your model. There are three ways to do this.

Check cache hits per request – The container doesn’t report prompt token details by default, so set 

SM_VLLM_ENABLE_PROMPT_TOKENS_DETAILS
to 
true
in the model environment. Each response then includes 
usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens
, the number of prompt tokens that were served from the KV cache. When you send a follow-up turn, or another request that starts the same way as an earlier one, a non-zero value shows that the request reached an instance that held its prefix.

Check model metrics in Amazon CloudWatch – Turn on detailed observability by adding 

--metrics-config '{"EnableDetailedObservability": true}'
when you create the endpoint configuration, using the SDK versions in Requirements and limits. SageMaker AI then publishes the model container’s metrics, including the KV cache hit rate and TTFT. Query them as described in Detailed observability with PromQL.

Compare with the strategy you would otherwise use – For most LLM workloads the real choice is between 

KV_AWARE
and 
PREFIX_AWARE
, so compare those two, and add a 
RANDOM
endpoint as a baseline. Use the same model, instance type, and instance count for each endpoint, and send the same prompts at the same concurrency for the same duration, so that the only difference is the routing strategy. Make sure your test reuses context the way your production traffic does, for example with multi-turn conversations or shared documents. If 
KV_AWARE
and 
PREFIX_AWARE
perform about the same for your traffic, prefix-aware routing is the simpler choice.

As an example of this comparison, we compared 

RANDOM
and 
KV_AWARE
on a small endpoint. We sent the same multi-turn workload to two endpoints that differ only in routing strategy. Each endpoint had two 
ml.g5.xlarge
instances serving 
Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507
on a supported container. Each run sent 128 requests: 32 simulated users, each asking 4 questions about a document chosen from 12 documents of about 7,400 tokens. Each question resends the conversation so far, so every question after the first can reuse cached context. We ran two pairs of runs, with 
RANDOM
first in pair 1 and 
KV_AWARE
first in pair 2, and used new documents for each pair so that both endpoints started with empty caches. Table 1 shows the results as pair 1 / pair 2.
MetricRANDOMKV_AWARE
CloudWatch ModelLatency average (ms)4,124 / 5,1001,235 / 1,314
CloudWatch ModelLatency p50 (ms)3,153 / 4,083656 / 700
CloudWatch ModelLatency p90 (ms)8,334 / 10,7463,213 / 3,535
CloudWatch ModelLatency p99 (ms)17,779 / 16,2496,876 / 7,238
Time to first token p50, questions 2–4 (ms)1,284 / 1,632237 / 245
Time to first token p90, questions 2–4 (ms)5,039 / 6,101456 / 367
