The client measured time to first token and run duration. The cache share is the sum of cached_tokens divided by the sum of prompt_tokens over a run

In both pairs, 

KV_AWARE
had lower CloudWatch ModelLatency (average 1,235 and 1,314 ms against 4,124 and 5,100 ms) and lower time to first token for questions 2–4 (p50 237 and 245 ms against 1,284 and 1,632 ms). Its cache share was higher, at 90 percent in both pairs against 76 and 70 percent. OverheadLatency, the time SageMaker AI spends outside the model container, was 14 to 19 ms higher on average with 
KV_AWARE
. This is one model, one instance type, and one workload with long shared documents, so measure your own traffic as described earlier in this section. Figure 3 shows the model latency charts that the SageMaker AI console displays for the two endpoints.

If neither does better than 

RANDOM
, check that prefix caching and KV cache events are turned on in the container, as described in Requirements and limits.

Example notebook

The example notebook applies the steps in this post to Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on two 

ml.g5.xlarge
 instances, the minimum for a single model endpoint, and on an inference component endpoint with two copies. It calls the endpoint with both APIs, shows in the container logs that follow-up requests are served from the KV cache, and doesn’t compare routing strategies. Run its cleanup cells at the end to avoid ongoing charges.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources you created. For an inference component endpoint, delete the inference components first (

delete-inference-component
), then the endpoint, endpoint configuration, and model (
delete-endpoint
, 
delete-endpoint-config
, 
delete-model
).

Practical guidance

These three practices help you keep KV-aware routing effective after you turn it on.

Monitor the KV cache hit rate – Keep detailed observability on after launch and watch the KV cache hit rate over time in the SageMaker AI Insights dashboard (Figure 2b), or query it with PromQL, as described in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.

Plan for cold starts – The first request with new context, such as a new document or the first turn of a conversation, has nothing cached on any instance. KV-aware routing speeds up the requests that follow, not the first one.

Plan for cache rebuilds during scaling and updates – As described in How KV-aware routing works, new instances start with empty caches. To soften the latency increase, use a rolling or blue/green update for single model endpoints, or a 

RollingUpdatePolicy
for inference components.

Conclusion

KV-aware routing gives SageMaker AI real-time endpoints a second way to send requests to where their prompts are cached. It uses the cache state that your model container reports, so it follows the cache when instances evict it under memory pressure. Prefix-aware routing from part 1 of this series remains the simpler choice for stable shared prompts, short contexts, and moderate load. SageMaker AI handles routing inside the endpoint for both strategies, so you don’t build or run a routing layer yourself. You turn it on with one environment variable in the model and 

"RoutingStrategy": "KV_AWARE"
in the endpoint configuration.

KV-aware routing is available today in all commercial AWS Regions that support SageMaker AI real-time inference, for endpoints that use a supported container. It is available at no additional charge. SageMaker AI runs and manages the cache index for you, and you pay only for the instances your endpoint uses. 

KV_AWARE
is a new value for the existing 
RoutingStrategy
field, so you don’t need a new configuration object, and older versions of the AWS CLI and Boto3 accept it. To get started, read the documentation, run the example notebook on a small endpoint, and then compare 
KV_AWARE
with 
PREFIX_AWARE
on a copy of your own traffic.

entries.title: Govern and discover records with common metadata in AWS Agent Registry
entries.summary: Custom metadata schemas in AWS Agent Registry let an administrator define typed, validated fields that every agent, MCP server, and skill must carry. This post follows an MCP record from schema definition through registration, enrichment, approval, and discovery, so teams govern and find resources with one shared set of facts.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Govern and discover records with common metadata in AWS Agent Registry

As organizations build more agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and skills, they need a consistent way to describe, govern, and find them. AWS Agent Registry provides a catalog for registering, approving, and discovering these resources and custom records. Each record carries a name, a description, a protocol descriptor, and an approval status. However, every organization has attributes and facts that it wants to track, and some are unique to that organization, such as its business units, resource owners, risk classifications, and development environments. Organizations want one common definition for each of these attributes, and they want every agent, MCP server, and skill in the registry to carry these facts. Until now, organizations had no way to define these facts in AWS Agent Registry and store them on each record.

Custom metadata schemas are now available in AWS Agent Registry. A custom metadata schema is a set of organization-defined key-value pairs that records in an AWS Agent Registry carry. An administrator defines the schema and applies it to the registry, and all records within the registry must then adhere to the schema. When publishers create or submit records, they supply values for the fields specified in the applicable schema, and AWS Agent Registry validates those values against the schema set by the admin. Approvers can rely on the validated values when reviewing a record, and consumers and agents can use them to discover and filter records. Administrators, publishers, security and governance teams, approvers, consumers, and agents all work from a shared set of facts to govern, discover, and understand the resources in their agentic fleet.

In this post, we follow the AnyCompany organization publishing an MCP server with custom schema definition, enriching that record, and making it available for discovery by humans or agents. We use an MCP server as the example, but the same steps apply to other record types.

How custom metadata works

With custom metadata, an organization can use standardized vocabulary for describing its resources. The registry administrator defines the custom metadata schema: field names, types, allowed values, and whether each field is required or optional. The registry enforces the schema on every record, so a field such as 

environment
has the same name and the same allowed values whichever team publishes the record.

The schema has common attributes that apply to every record type, and you can add dedicated fields that only apply to specific record types. Each field is Text, Enum, URL, or Boolean.

  • When a record is created or updated, the registry validates the custom metadata against the schema set up by the admin.

    • If a record is created without any custom metadata, AWS Agent Registry saves it as 

      NON_COMPLIANT
      . A team can save work in progress this way, but it can’t submit the record for approval until it has the required fields and values.

    • If a record includes custom metadata with an unknown field, a missing required field, or an invalid value, AWS Agent Registry rejects it with a 

      ValidationException
      .

  • GetRegistryRecord
    returns the record’s custom metadata values and its compliance status. (
    COMPLIANT
    means that the values match the administrator’s schema. It is not an approval. The approvers make that decision.)

  • Discovery APIs also allow filtering records based on custom attributes.

What custom metadata makes possible

Because teams can describe the AWS Agent Registry records with the same fields and values, the registry can support and scale governance and compliance.

Ownership and operations

Fields such as 

environment
(
prod
, 
staging
, or 
dev
), 
businessUnit
, 
ownerTeam
, 
supportContact
, and 
costCenter
record where a resource runs, who is responsible for it, and who pays for it. A configuration management database (CMDB) ID links the record to your existing inventory, and a support-tier field sets expectations for anyone who depends on the resource.

Security and compliance

Data classification, compliance scope such as Payment Card Industry (PCI) or Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), risk tier, scan status, and a scan report URL turn an approval into a check of structured evidence. Your existing scanners, CMDB sync jobs, and classification tools write these values through the API before a record is submitted. You can build your record approval process or automation using these values, as this post shows.

Better discovery

Custom metadata values are indexed for search. A consumer or agent can combine a natural-language query with specific metadata filters, such as 

environment=prod AND businessUnit=payments AND securityScanStatus=PASSED
. Only approved records are returned, so a record that matches the filters but hasn’t been approved stays out of the results. Figure 1 shows how each role, from administrator to consumer, moves a record through schema definition, registration, enrichment, approval, and discovery.

Walkthrough of an MCP record from registration to discovery

AnyCompany operates 

anycompany-governed-registry
, an AWS Agent Registry without auto-approval. Its payments team publishes an MCP record, 
payments-ledger-mcp
, a read-only server for ledger lookups. Existing security and inventory systems enrich this MCP record before an approval function decides whether consumers can discover it.

The five numbered steps in Figure 2 match the walkthrough: define, register, enrich and submit, review, then discover.

Prerequisites

To follow the walkthrough, you need:

  • An AWS account in a supported AWS Region.

  • AWS credentials available to Boto3 and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for AWS Agent Registry.

  • Python 3.11 or later and boto3 1.43.113 or later.

  • The sample implementation is in the GitHub repo.

The snippets are shortened: 

cp
and 
dp
are the 
agent-registry-control
and 
agent-registry
boto3 clients. The sample repository has the complete code.

Step 1: AWS Agent Registry admin defines the custom metadata schema for the registry

AnyCompany’s admin creates a registry with a custom metadata schema that every record must follow.

  • Every record must have its 

    environment
    , 
    businessUnit
    , and 
    securityScanStatus
    fields.

  • Records can also carry optional fields that the publisher or automation fills in later: 

    ownerTeam
    , 
    cmdbId
    , 
    dataClassification
    , and 
    securityScanReportUrl
    .

  • MCP servers also record their 

    networkEgress
    , which is optional.

Figure 3 shows this schema and the values 

payments-ledger-mcp
will carry once enrichment completes in Step 3. The empty 
autoApprovalRules
list means that the registry approves nothing on its own. Every submitted record stays in 
Pending approval
until someone or something approves it. You decide whether that is done by automated checks you build (Step 4 uses an AWS Lambda function), a human approver, or both.

Administrators can also review the schema in the AWS Agent Registry console. Figure 4 shows the common attributes and the MCP-specific field as they appear on the registry’s details page.

Step 2: The publisher registers the server

The payments team’s pipeline registers 

payments-ledger-mcp
with its custom metadata. Its first attempt uses 
production
instead of one of the administrator’s allowed values.

The registry rejects the record. After the pipeline sends 

prod
, the record is created as a compliant draft. This is how the schema keeps every team using the same values.

Step 3: Automation adds additional metadata and submits

Next, AnyCompany’s automation adds what its own systems know: the result from its security scanner, the asset ID from its CMDB, and the approved data classification. It then submits the record for approval.

An update replaces the whole metadata map, so the automation reads the current values, adds its own, and writes them back together. In the sample, the scanner and CMDB calls are stubs that you replace with your own tools. The registry sends a pending-approval event to Amazon EventBridge. In Step 4, a rule that you create passes the event to your approval function.

Step 4: The approval automation decides from the evidence

When the record moves to Pending approval, AWS Agent Registry sends an event to Amazon EventBridge, and an Amazon EventBridge rule is set to invoke a custom AWS Lambda function. Figure 5 shows the console view of 

payments-ledger-mcp
, with the custom metadata values that the approval function reads for its check.

The function reads the record’s custom metadata and compliance status to check that the record is 

COMPLIANT
, the scan 
PASSED
, a 
cmdbId
is present, and the data is public or internal. 
payments-ledger-mcp
passes all four, so the function approves. A record that fails a check is rejected, and the reason names the failed check. In your production systems, you can choose to route records that need a human review, such as those with confidential or restricted data, for manual review instead of being rejected.

Step 5: Consumers find the records from AWS Agent Registry with custom metadata fields as filters

A developer looking for a ledger tool searches the registry and filters on the same fields the administrator defined.

The search returns 

payments-ledger-mcp
because it’s approved and matches all three filters. Agents can run the same search through the registry’s MCP endpoint, 
https://agentregistry..api.aws/registry//mcp
, which offers search, list, and get as MCP tools. In the GitHub sample, a Strands agent connects to the AWS Registry MCP endpoint and uses a model on Amazon Bedrock. Its system prompt lists the custom metadata fields to filter records on. The agent turns a plain-language request, such as “a production MCP server for payments ledger lookups that passed its security scan”, into a filtered search. It answers with 
payments-ledger-mcp
.

Developers and agents query the same fields the administrator defined, and the approval function checked, so both find only servers that meet your governance rules.

Design the schema for long-term use

Treat the schema as your organization’s shared vocabulary:

  • Agree on the vocabulary first. Settle field names and allowed values with the teams that publish and approve records before you create the schema. Schema changes are additive: you can add fields, add allowed values, or make an optional field required, but you can’t rename, remove, or retype a field.

  • Expect existing records to lag behind schema changes made after the records were added to the registry. Existing records aren’t rewritten. A record that no longer matches the schema is reported as 

    NON_COMPLIANT
    and keeps its approval status. The record stays approved, but its next update must meet the new schema. Editing an approved record creates a draft that must be submitted for approval again, and the submit fails until every required field has a value. Until a curator approves the new revision, consumers keep seeing the approved one.

  • Put each field at the right level. Use common attributes for questions that apply to every record type, and record-type fields for record-specific facts such as autonomy level for agents.

  • Pick the type that fits the field. Use Enums for decision fields that need consistent spelling, Text for external identifiers, and URL for evidence stored behind the source system’s access controls.

  • Make a field required only when the publisher can assign a value at registration. For a value that your continuous integration (CI) or automation provides after the record is published, allow an interim value, for example 

    PENDING
    . In this post, the scan runs after registration, so 
    securityScanStatus
    has three values: 
    PENDING
    , 
    PASSED
    , and 
    FAILED
    . The publisher writes 
    PENDING
    , and the enrichment automation replaces it.

  • Keep sensitive details out. Leave secrets, internal endpoints, and detailed findings out of broadly readable metadata.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how to add custom metadata in AWS Agent Registry to give every record a common set of facts, such as its environment, owning business unit, data classification, and security scan status. Using one MCP server, we showed an administrator defining the schema, a publisher and existing automation filling in the values, an approval function that you build in AWS Lambda deciding approval, and a consumer finding the approved server with metadata filters. Because the administrator owns the schema, every team uses the same fields and values, and that consistency is what makes approvals and searches in AWS Agent Registry dependable.

  • Try it yourself: Use the sample at GitHub repo.

  • Go deeper: Read the AWS Agent Registry Developer Guide and custom metadata API reference.

  • Availability: See supported AWS Regions.

entries.title: Secure OAuth patterns for Snowflake Cortex AI through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
entries.summary: When an AI agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore calls Snowflake Cortex AI over MCP, how does it authenticate? This post walks through three OAuth patterns we tested on AgentCore Identity: Snowflake OAuth, three-legged OAuth with a corporate IdP, and two-legged OAuth, so you can match your organization's identity, audit, and compliance needs.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Secure OAuth patterns for Snowflake Cortex AI through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Enterprises today need a clear way to extend their authentication and authorization controls into the agentic layer, often requiring either broad service account permissions or custom-built auth integrations that add operational overhead. When an AI agent running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model) needs to call the Snowflake-managed MCP server (which exposes Snowflake Cortex Agents as one of its tool types) through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the first question enterprises must answer is: how does the agent authenticate? In this post, we walk through three Open Authorization (OAuth) configurations we tested on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Snowflake OAuth (per-user, no external Identity Provider, or IdP), three-legged OAuth with a third-party Identity Provider (corporate single sign-on, or SSO), and two-legged OAuth with a third-party Identity Provider (shared service user). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also supports an on-behalf-of (OBO) grant (TOKEN_EXCHANGE) that delivers per-user identity for unattended workloads without a consent prompt. We focus on the three configurations we tested end-to-end, flagging where OBO fits as we go. By the end, you will be able to identify which pattern suits your enterprise scenario.

Solution overview

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, connects AI agents to external tool providers through MCP server targets. It targets the Snowflake-managed MCP server, which surfaces Cortex Search and Cortex Analyst as MCP tools that an MCP-aware client can discover and invoke. Rather than acting as a wrapper, the Gateway aggregates the capabilities of its configured targets into a single unified catalog, which it presents to the agent as one tools/list response.

The core focus of this post is the outbound authentication for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway: how it obtains and presents OAuth tokens to the Snowflake-managed MCP server. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity acts as the credential broker: the Gateway obtains a workload token by calling GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT (because the Gateway uses JSON Web Token (JWT) inbound authentication), then calls GetResourceOauth2Token against the configured provider. AgentCore Identity owns the token vault, the token refresh, and the user-to-token binding, and it fetches, caches, and refreshes tokens automatically.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity supports three OAuth configurations spanning two grant types (authorization_code and client_credentials):

  • Snowflake OAuth: Snowflake acts as its own OAuth authorization server. Each user authenticates directly to Snowflake through the Authorization Code grant (3LO). No external identity provider is needed.
  • Three-legged OAuth using a third-party Identity Provider: Users authenticate through corporate SSO with the Authorization Code grant. Snowflake trusts IdP-issued JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) through its External OAuth security integration.
  • Two-legged OAuth pattern using a third-party IdP: A shared service user authenticates through the client_credentials grant of the IdP. No user interaction or consent is required, which is ideal for machine-to-machine workloads.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also offers an API-key credential provider (which supports Snowflake Programmatic Access Tokens). We focus on OAuth here for per-user attribution and automatic token refresh. Each configuration uses a credential provider in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity (CustomOauth2, OktaOauth2, or MicrosoftOauth2) and a corresponding security integration on the Snowflake side.

Note: We tested these patterns with the Snowflake-managed MCP server using Okta and Microsoft Entra ID. Patterns 2 and 3 (external IdP) follow standard OAuth flows, so they can extend to other OAuth-protected MCP servers, but validate the token claims, scopes, and audience settings for your SaaS provider. Only Pattern 1 is Snowflake-specific, because it relies on Snowflake’s built-in OAuth authorization server. The Snowflake-specific elements are the OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER issuer-lock parameter, the session:role: / session:scope: grammar, BLOCKED_ROLES_LIST, LOGIN_NAME / EMAIL_ADDRESS mapping, and QUERY_HISTORY attribution. If your SaaS exposes its own internal OAuth server, you configure outbound OAuth the same way as Snowflake OAuth.

PatternOAuth grantAgentCore Identity credential provider vendorSnowflake security integrationSnowflake query identity mapping
Snowflake OAuth – 3LOauthorization_codeCustom provider (CustomOauth2)TYPE = OAUTH, OAUTH_CLIENT = CUSTOMThe real user, with their assigned role
3LO with external IdPauthorization_codeBuilt-in provider (such as OktaOauth2, MicrosoftOauth2)TYPE = EXTERNAL_OAUTH + OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER (set with ALTER ACCOUNT / DATABASE / SCHEMA); EXTERNAL_OAUTH_TYPE = OKTA / AZURE / PING_FEDERATE / CUSTOMThe real user, with their assigned role
2LO with external IdPclient_credentialsBuilt-in provider (such as OktaOauth2, MicrosoftOauth2) or CustomOauth2TYPE = EXTERNAL_OAUTH + OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER (set with ALTER ACCOUNT / DATABASE / SCHEMA); EXTERNAL_OAUTH_TYPE = OKTA / AZURE / PING_FEDERATE / CUSTOMA shared Snowflake service user

Notes:

  • 2LO does not require a built-in vendor. CustomOauth2 with the CLIENT_CREDENTIALS grant can work with your choice of OAuth 2.0 authorization server.
  • When Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway brokers the token (the pattern in this post), Snowflake validates it through the TYPE = EXTERNAL_OAUTH security integration. Setting OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER (with ALTER ACCOUNT, DATABASE, or SCHEMA) is what lets direct MCP clients auto-discover your IdP through the Protected Resource Metadata endpoint, and it issuer-locks the MCP endpoint to that integration.
  • If you set OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER to issuer-lock an MCP scope to an external IdP (Pattern 2), Snowflake OAuth tokens (Pattern 1) are rejected for MCP servers in that scope and do not fall back. If you need both patterns in one account, set this parameter per schema or database so each scope resolves to the right authorization server.

Solution architecture

The following diagram shows the solution we built and the components it uses: a user-facing AI application, a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Bedrock for reasoning, with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails redacting personally identifiable information (PII) from prompts and responses, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability, over policy documents in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with the Snowflake-managed MCP server as its target, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity holding the token vault. The outbound OAuth path has the same shape in all three patterns: the Gateway resolves a token through AgentCore Identity, which obtains and renews it from an authorization server, and the Gateway then presents that token to the Snowflake-managed MCP server. What changes between the patterns is which authorization server issues the token and under which grant: Snowflake’s own built-in OAuth server, or a third-party IdP. Those differences are set out in the Pattern comparison table, and each pattern’s runtime flow has its own sequence diagram later in this post.

Pattern analysis

The following sections examine each pattern in detail: the authentication flow, configuration steps, and trade-offs to help you select the right approach for your use case.

Pattern 1: Snowflake OAuth (three-legged)

The Snowflake OAuth pattern uses a three-legged OAuth (3LO) flow to deliver per-user authentication without requiring an external identity provider. Each user authenticates to Snowflake with their own credentials, consents to a specific Snowflake role, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity caches that user’s access and refresh tokens. Every subsequent Snowflake call executes as that user, and QUERY_HISTORY records their real username. Note that per-role consent is not the default. The Snowflake-managed MCP server advertises session:role:all and falls back to DEFAULT_ROLE, so you set OAUTH_SCOPES_SUPPORTED (an account-, database-, or schema-level parameter set with ALTER) to narrow the role scope the server advertises, and restrict ALLOWED_ROLES_LIST on the integration to enforce which roles a user can consent to (PRE_AUTHORIZED_ROLES_LIST does the opposite: it lists roles that skip the consent step).

What makes this pattern appealing is its simplicity: no external identity provider is required. Snowflake acts as both the authorization server and the resource server, exposing its own built-in OAuth endpoints (/oauth/authorize and /oauth/token-request). Setup follows a specific order, because the callback URL does not exist until the credential provider is created. The administrator first creates the CustomOauth2 credential provider in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity with placeholder client credentials and records the callbackUrl that AgentCore Identity returns. That callbackUrl is then registered as the redirect URI on a Snowflake security integration created with TYPE = OAUTH and OAUTH_CLIENT = CUSTOM. Finally, the administrator updates the credential provider with the real client ID and secret issued by Snowflake and configures the provider’s oauthDiscovery with explicit authorization server metadata: the issuer (the Snowflake account URL), the authorization endpoint (/oauth/authorize), and the token endpoint (/oauth/token-request).

The following screenshot shows the configuration steps for credential provider vendors in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity with Snowflake OAuth (3LO) settings.

Next, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway configuration points to the Snowflake-managed MCP server endpoint and references the custom Snowflake OAuth for outbound authentication.

The following sequence diagram shows the runtime authorization flow for the Snowflake OAuth pattern.

The Snowflake OAuth authorization flow works as follows:

  • When a tool call requires a Snowflake token, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway obtains a workload token by calling GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT and calls GetResourceOauth2Token to check the token vault of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity for the user. If no token is cached, the Gateway returns a JSON-RPC error code -32042 carrying a URL elicitation. That authorization URL belongs to AgentCore Identity and is 
    session-URI-bound
    . The client opens that URL in the user’s browser, which is routed to Snowflake’s built-in authorization server (/oauth/authorize) and shown a Snowflake login screen.
  • The user enters their Snowflake credentials and is presented with a consent screen asking them to authorize access using a specific Snowflake role (for example, ANALYST_ROLE). Role names in the requested scope must be uppercase (for example, session:role:ANALYST_ROLE).
  • Upon consent, Snowflake’s authorization server returns an authorization code to the callback URL of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity. AgentCore Identity then redirects the user’s browser to the return URL with the session URI.
  • AgentCore Identity completes the code exchange only after the application calls CompleteResourceTokenAuth with the user identity and session URI (valid for 10 minutes). This step binds the code to the originating request and blocks authorization-URL hijacking. The return URL used here is registered by calling UpdateWorkloadIdentity. In production, the endpoint at that URL is hosted either by your web application or, for gateways with JWT inbound authentication, by the AgentCore Identity Consent Portal (
    /connect/callback
    ). The agentcore dev CLI hosts it only for local development. AgentCore Identity then exchanges the code at Snowflake’s token endpoint (/oauth/token-request) for an access token and, optionally, a refresh token.
  • When the client retries the tool call, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway retrieves the cached access token from AgentCore Identity and presents it to the Snowflake-managed MCP server. Snowflake validates the token and creates a user session scoped to the consented role. The consented scope controls the primary role only. Because secondary roles are governed by the integration, set OAUTH_USE_SECONDARY_ROLES = NONE (the default) so the session cannot carry more privilege than the consented role, which the IMPLICIT setting would allow.

Access tokens are short-lived. By default, they last 600 seconds (maximum 3600). When an access token expires, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity automatically uses the refresh token to obtain a new access token, with no user interaction required. If the security integration is configured to prevent refreshing tokens, the user must re-authorize through the consent screen. Refresh-token lifetime is controlled by OAUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN_VALIDITY. The reference implementation sets it to 86400 seconds (1 day), and Snowflake allows up to 90 days. OAUTH_ISSUE_REFRESH_TOKENS (default TRUE) governs whether refresh tokens are issued at all.

Note: By default, Snowflake helps prevent the ACCOUNTADMIN, ORGADMIN, GLOBALORGADMIN, and SECURITYADMIN roles from being used with OAuth integrations. This is controlled by BLOCKED_ROLES_LIST for Snowflake OAuth (and EXTERNAL_OAUTH_BLOCKED_ROLES_LIST for External OAuth), applies to all three patterns, and covers the primary role only. With OAUTH_USE_SECONDARY_ROLES = IMPLICIT, secondary roles can still carry these privileged roles.

Considerations

The Snowflake OAuth pattern is the simplest path to per-user audit trails. It needs no external IdP configuration and no additional vendor dependency. It is best suited for scenarios where:

  • Users already have Snowflake credentials and are comfortable signing in directly.
  • You want per-user attribution in QUERY_HISTORY without an external identity provider.
  • You are in a proof-of-concept phase and want to validate the per-user model quickly.
  • Compliance requirements mandate individual accountability, so each query must be traceable to a specific user, not a shared service user.
  • You prefer to manage user lifecycle (provisioning, deprovisioning, role grants) entirely within Snowflake.
  • You want to avoid token claim mapping complexities. Snowflake issues tokens and knows exactly which user they represent.

Pattern 2: Three-legged OAuth (3LO) using a third-party Identity Provider (IdP)

This pattern combines per-user authentication with corporate single sign-on. Users sign in through the external IdP, which enforces multi-factor authentication (MFA), conditional access, and session policies. The IdP-issued JWT is presented to Snowflake, which validates it through its External OAuth security integration (optionally issuer-locked to the MCP server’s schema, database, or account with OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER). Snowflake verifies the issuer, audience, and signature through a JSON Web Key Set (JWKS). It then maps a configurable claim, set with EXTERNAL_OAUTH_TOKEN_USER_MAPPING_CLAIM (sub for Okta, upn for Microsoft Entra ID), to a Snowflake user’s LOGIN_NAME or EMAIL_ADDRESS (with EXTERNAL_OAUTH_SNOWFLAKE_USER_MAPPING_ATTRIBUTE), and runs the query as that user. The security integration parameter values are case-sensitive.

The key difference from Pattern 1: the authorization server is your corporate IdP (such as Okta, Microsoft Entra ID), not Snowflake. Snowflake remains the resource server. Users authenticate with the same credentials and policies they use for every other corporate application. No separate Snowflake passwords are required.

On the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore side, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity provides built-in credential provider vendors for popular identity providers (for example, OktaOauth2 and MicrosoftOauth2). These vendors accept the client ID, client secret, and IdP endpoints through includedOauth2ProviderConfig, compared to the generic CustomOauth2 provider used in Pattern 1. The Snowflake-managed MCP server uses pre-registered OAuth clients, so you register each client ID and secret in advance, which is why the create, record callbackUrl, register, update sequence is required.

Next, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway configuration points to the Snowflake-managed MCP server endpoint and references the Okta credential provider for outbound authentication.

The following sequence diagram shows the runtime authorization flow for the three-legged OAuth pattern with an external IdP.

Snowflake’s External OAuth security integration flow works as follows:

  • When a tool call requires a Snowflake token, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway obtains a workload token by calling GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT and calls GetResourceOauth2Token to check the token vault of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity for the user. If no token is cached, the Gateway returns a JSON-RPC error code -32042 carrying a URL elicitation. That authorization URL belongs to AgentCore Identity and is 
    session-URI-bound
    , not the IdP’s. The client opens that URL in the user’s browser, and AgentCore Identity routes the user to the IdP.
  • The user authenticates through the third-party IdP with corporate SSO (including MFA) and consents to the requested scopes. For Okta, the role scope takes the form session:role:ANALYST_ROLE. Microsoft Entra ID delegated flows use session:scope: instead.
  • The IdP returns an authorization code to the callback URL of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, and AgentCore Identity redirects the user’s browser to the return URL with the session URI. Only after the application calls CompleteResourceTokenAuth to validate the user identity and session URI does AgentCore Identity exchange the code for an access token (and a refresh token, if the IdP issues one) and cache them in the per-user token vault.
  • When the client retries the tool call (and on later calls), Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway retrieves the cached IdP-issued JWT from Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity and presents it to the Snowflake-managed MCP server. Snowflake validates the token through its External OAuth integration: it verifies the JWKS signature and audience (aud) claim, maps the configured user claim (sub for Okta, upn for Microsoft Entra ID) to the Snowflake user, and executes the query as the authenticated user. Snowflake does not call the IdP at runtime. It validates tokens locally using the IdP’s published JWKS signing keys.
  • When the access token expires, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity automatically refreshes it using the cached refresh token, if one was issued (for Okta, request the offline_access scope). No user interaction is required until the refresh token expires.

Token lifetime governance: Unlike Pattern 1 where Snowflake controls token lifetimes, access token and refresh token lifetimes are governed by the IdP, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity handles the refresh transparently. If a refresh token was issued, the user re-authenticates only when it expires, based on the IdP’s session policy. Otherwise, the user re-authenticates when the access token expires.

Considerations

Choose three-legged OAuth (3LO) with a third-party IdP when:

  • Your organization or security team requires all authentication to flow through corporate SSO for centralized MFA, conditional access, and session management.
  • You want to use existing IdP features such as group-based role mapping, session timeout policies, and geo-based conditional access rules.
  • You need per-user audit trails in Snowflake’s QUERY_HISTORY.
  • You want uniform security policy enforcement across all applications, including AI agents.
  • You need centralized access control. Disabling a user in the IdP helps prevent new Snowflake authorizations, though cached tokens stay valid until they expire. To force a user to re-authorize, the application can pass forceAuthentication=true on the next request, which clears the stored refresh token and starts a new authorization flow. To revoke access outright, revoke the grant at the IdP or in Snowflake.

Pattern 3: Two-legged OAuth (2LO) using a third-party Identity Provider (IdP)

The two-legged OAuth pattern uses the OAuth 2.0 client_credentials grant. This is a machine-to-machine flow with no user interaction. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity obtains a JWT from the IdP using the configured client ID and client secret, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway presents it to Snowflake, which executes the requests under a shared service user, regardless of which end user initiated the query.

This pattern is the most operationally direct: no consent screens, no per-user token vaults, no browser redirects. The users follow the same code path. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity fetches and caches the client_credentials token automatically, and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway presents it on every outbound call to the Snowflake-managed MCP server.

The key difference from Patterns 1 and 2: there is no per-user identity propagation. Snowflake’s QUERY_HISTORY records a single service user for queries. The trade-off is operational simplicity at the cost of per-user audit granularity. On the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore side, the credential provider uses the client_credentials grant type: either a built-in vendor (OktaOauth2, MicrosoftOauth2) or the generic CustomOauth2 provider. Configuration requires the IdP’s token endpoint, client ID, and client secret. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity fetches a token from the IdP on the first tool call (when the Gateway calls GetResourceOauth2Token), caches it, and, because client_credentials issues no refresh token, requests a fresh one before expiry. No agent-level code changes are required.

Next, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway configuration references the Snowflake-managed MCP server endpoint and the two-legged OAuth credential provider for outbound authentication.

The following sequence diagram shows the runtime authorization flow for the two-legged OAuth pattern.

Snowflake’s External OAuth security integration 2LO flow works as follows:

  • When a tool call requires a Snowflake token, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway obtains a workload token by calling GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT and calls GetResourceOauth2Token on the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity credential provider. If a valid token is cached, Identity returns it immediately.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity calls the third-party IdP’s token endpoint using the client_credentials grant with the configured client ID and client secret. For Okta, the requested scope includes the Snowflake role (for example, session:role:MCP_GATEWAY_ROLE). For Microsoft Entra ID, the client requests the api:
    ///.default
    scope and the role arrives in the roles claim from an app role whose value is session:role:MCP_GATEWAY_ROLE.
  • The IdP returns an access token (a JWT, with no refresh token) whose aud claim is the Snowflake account URL or an additional value listed in EXTERNAL_OAUTH_AUDIENCE_LIST (for Microsoft Entra ID, typically the Application ID URI). For Okta, the sub claim is the client ID. For Microsoft Entra ID, the client ID is carried in appid/azp while sub holds the service principal’s object ID (a GUID), so with Entra, LOGIN_NAME must map to that GUID.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway presents the JWT to the Snowflake-managed MCP server. Snowflake validates the token through its External OAuth integration (optionally issuer-locked with OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER, as in Pattern 2). It verifies the signature through EXTERNAL_OAUTH_JWS_KEYS_URL (or EXTERNAL_OAUTH_RSA_PUBLIC_KEY), the issuer through EXTERNAL_OAUTH_ISSUER, and the aud claim against the Snowflake account URL plus any additional values in EXTERNAL_OAUTH_AUDIENCE_LIST (these security integration parameter values are case-sensitive). Snowflake then maps the sub claim to a Snowflake service user through LOGIN_NAME and executes the query under that service user’s role. As in Pattern 2, Snowflake validates the token locally and does not call the IdP at runtime.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity caches the token in the token vault (shared across users, not per user). Subsequent calls reuse it, and Identity requests a new token with the client_credentials grant before it expires.

Because the two-legged OAuth target needs no user consent, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway connects to the Snowflake-managed MCP server at target-creation time and discovers tools through implicit sync during target creation. In the 3-legged OAuth patterns (Patterns 1 and 2), the Gateway target supports two creation methods: (1) an admin completes the authorization code flow so tools are discovered by implicit sync, or (2) the admin provides the tool schema upfront. (Discovery behavior is a ListingMode property of the target, not a property of the grant type.)

Considerations

The two-legged OAuth pattern is preferred for automated, unattended, and batch workloads. It is ideal when:

  • Your workload is machine-to-machine: scheduled jobs, background pipelines, or system-level agents with no human in the loop.
  • Per-user identity isn’t required, and a shared service user is acceptable for audit purposes.
  • You need the most direct operational model: no consent flows, per-user token management, or browser redirects.
  • The Gateway can connect to Snowflake and discover MCP tools by implicit sync at target-creation time, without waiting for user interaction.
  • All users share the same data access rights under a single Snowflake role.

Accept these trade-offs:

  • Because every request runs as the shared service user, Snowflake’s row-level security and column masking policies apply that user’s permissions to requests. Policies keyed on CURRENT_USER() and CURRENT_ROLE() all resolve to that single service user and its one role, which is the strongest case for the on-behalf-of (OBO) approach.
  • There is no user-level token revocation. To cut off access, revoke the client credentials at the IdP or disable the Snowflake security integration.
  • If credentials are compromised, agent access is affected. Rotate client secrets regularly and restrict the service user to least-privilege access.

Pattern comparison
