¹ MCP protocol revision: for the three-legged patterns (Patterns 1 and 2), the gateway pins 2025-11-25 in its supported MCP revisions, which the URL-mode elicitation (-32042) handshake requires. The reference 2LO gateway (Pattern 3) does not pin it, because 2LO has no elicitation step. On accounts that are not enabled for MCP version updates, the supported set is fixed when the gateway is created.

² Works unattended: Patterns 1 and 2 run unattended only until the refresh token expires. Re-consent then requires a live browser, the same user, and completion inside the 10-minute authorization window (CompleteResourceTokenAuth), which is why 3LO is unsuitable for fully unattended scheduled jobs. Pattern 3 (2LO) has no refresh token and no consent step, so it runs unattended indefinitely.

The three configurations in this post cover two grant types: authorization_code (Patterns 1 and 2) and client_credentials (Pattern 3). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also supports on-behalf-of (OBO) token exchange (TOKEN_EXCHANGE), which delivers per-user identity for unattended workloads without a consent prompt.

OBO exchanges an inbound user token for a Snowflake-scoped token that preserves the real user’s identity, so QUERY_HISTORY attributes each query to the actual user, while keeping the unattended, machine-to-machine flow of Pattern 3 (no browser redirect, no consent screen). On the Snowflake side it uses the same TYPE = EXTERNAL_OAUTH integration as Patterns 2 and 3 (optionally issuer-locked with OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER). On the AgentCore side it is configured on the OAuth credential provider through onBehalfOfTokenExchangeConfig (grant mode TOKEN_EXCHANGE for Okta/RFC 8693, or JWT_AUTHORIZATION_GRANT for Microsoft Entra). OBO uses the External OAuth path (Patterns 2 and 3).

OBO is generally available on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, but it was outside the scope of the three configurations we tested for this post.

Try it yourself

To see these patterns in action, we built a financial-services credit-risk assessment agent as a reference workload. A single agent combines bank policy documents in Amazon S3 (through Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases) with customer data in Snowflake. It assesses loan eligibility, searches customer profiles, and queries account and transaction data. The demo exercises three MCP tools (Cortex Search, Cortex Analyst, and SQL Execution) across all three OAuth configurations for side-by-side comparison in your own AWS account.

Though the demo is financial services, the patterns work across healthcare, supply chain, insurance, and more. All three implementations are public and deploy end-to-end through a single 

deploy.sh
script:
  • Snowflake OAuth (3LO): amazon-bedrock-agentcore-snowflake-mcp-gateway-3lo.
  • 3LO with external IdP: amazon-bedrock-agentcore-snowflake-mcp-gateway-3lo-okta.
  • 2LO with external IdP: amazon-bedrock-agentcore-snowflake-mcp-gateway.

Note: For demonstration purposes, the reference implementations expose SYSTEM_EXECUTE_SQL on the same MCP server as the Cortex Agent. Snowflake recommends exposing a Cortex Agent as the only client-facing tool for governed business questions. If direct SQL is required, place it on a separate MCP server with a dedicated least-privileged role.

Conclusion

In this post, we walked through three OAuth configurations for authenticating AI agents to Snowflake Cortex AI over MCP through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. Snowflake OAuth offers the simplest path to per-user audit trails with no external IdP dependency. Three-legged OAuth with an external IdP adds corporate SSO, centralized MFA, and conditional access while preserving per-user identity. Two-legged OAuth with an external IdP serves machine-to-machine through a shared service user.

Across all three patterns, the agent code and the Snowflake MCP tool set stay unchanged. The OAuth wiring differs in four specific ways:

  • The grant type flips: authorization_code for Patterns 1 and 2, client_credentials for Pattern 3.
  • AUTHORIZATION_CODE targets need a return URL, set as defaultReturnUrl on the target and optionally overridden per request. 2LO targets need none.
  • 3LO target creation requires implicit sync or an upfront tool schema, whereas a 2LO target syncs its tools during target creation with no user authorization step.
  • OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER can be set for Patterns 2 and 3 to issuer-lock an MCP scope to the external IdP and to let direct MCP clients auto-discover it. It is left unset for Pattern 1. When it is set, Patterns 1 and 2 cannot share one scope, as noted earlier.

Beyond these four, only the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity credential provider (CustomOauth2, OktaOauth2, or MicrosoftOauth2) and the Snowflake security integration differ. Understanding these differences in grant type, token issuance, user mapping, and audit behavior equips you to select the right OAuth configuration for your compliance, operational, and user-experience needs.

To get started, explore the reference implementation in our GitHub repository. For more on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, visit the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore service detail page or the Developer Guide.

entries.title: Announcing AI data preparation capabilities in Amazon SageMaker: Build high-quality datasets for model development workflows
entries.summary: Amazon SageMaker AI now offers AI data preparation capabilities for building high-quality training and evaluation data. Generate synthetic examples, assess and improve datasets, auto-label at scale, and bring in expert review through Python SDK APIs and an agent skill, all from your own notebook or IDE.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Announcing AI data preparation capabilities in Amazon SageMaker: Build high-quality datasets for model development workflows

Teams that ship generative AI to production know that a model is only as good as its data. That is why preparing high-quality training and evaluation data comes first. Fine-tuning an open-weight model, running reinforcement learning, or building an evaluation suite all depend on data that is accurate, well-labeled, and representative of your task. For narrow, well-defined tasks, a smaller model customized on clean, task-specific data can often match or exceed the accuracy of a larger general-purpose model prompted into shape, at a lower cost per inference.

In practice, though, preparing that data is often the slowest part of the project. Labeled examples are scarce or expensive, and privacy rules limit what you can use. Quality problems such as duplicates, label noise, and answer leakage go unnoticed until a training run disappoints, and every training technique expects data in its own format. As a result, data scientists spend weeks wrangling data instead of building models.

Today, we’re expanding Amazon SageMaker AI with new AI data preparation capabilities for model development workflows. You can generate synthetic examples, assess and improve existing datasets, and bring expert feedback into the process through Python SDK APIs and the AWS AI-ML agent skill. You work in your notebook or IDE, with specifications and code that you can inspect and change.

Prepare data without hand-building pipelines

With AI Data Preparation capabilities, you don’t need to stitch together labeling tools, generation scripts, and validation jobs. Each capability is a standalone building block. You can use one of them on its own or chain them together according to the workflow you want.

  • Auto-labeling: Label data at scale from an unlabeled dataset, a small labeled seed set, or no labels at all. Built-in task types include classification, named entity recognition, extractive question answering, ordinal rating, and summarization, and you can define custom tasks. You describe the task in a short labeling spec, which is validated against your own examples before the full dataset is labeled. For tasks with a fixed set of possible answers, such as classification, named entity recognition, and extractive question answering, a jury of several models labels each row, and their level of agreement becomes that row’s confidence score.
  • Human review: Rows below your confidence threshold go to a review queue in Amazon SageMaker Studio, which uses the open-source Label Studio Community Edition. Outside subject matter experts can access the review app through the link in the partner app box in SageMaker Studio. Reviewer corrections feed back into auto-labeling, and you can generate consensus metrics and labeling reports.
  • Synthetic data generation: Generate training, evaluation, and test data from a specification. You can ground the output in your own seed data and documents, and the service generates a code-based data generation pipeline that you can review, modify, reuse, and scale.
  • Data quality evaluation: Check datasets against your own business rules, built-in metrics, and LLM-as-a-judge metrics. Find duplicates and near-duplicates, and surface issues you didn’t think to check for, such as label noise or answer leakage.
  • Data transformation: Clean and reshape data for your target training technique. Describe the change in plain language and have the code generated for you, use built-in operations such as dedupe, merge, split, and filter, or run your own Python at scale.

You work wherever you already work. Use the SageMaker Python SDK directly or provide your coding agent the AI-ML skill in the agent toolkit and let your agent invoke the APIs according to established data science best practices. Describe what you need, and the agent selects and runs the right capability in SageMaker Studio JupyterLab, Kiro, or your local IDE with your coding assistant of choice.

For teams building specialized models, the hardest part is often finding enough task-specific data. Splunk, a Cisco company, faced exactly this when building evaluation models for its Agent Observability product.

“For Splunk Agent Observability, our ability to train robust GenAI Eval models relies on access to high-quality, diverse datasets which are hard to curate for very specific tasks. Amazon SageMaker AI data preparation capabilities for synthetic data generation is meaningfully helping us scale these capabilities. We’ve been able to generate statistically representative synthetic datasets reliably and fast, while preserving the underlying patterns our models depend on. The seamless integration with the rest of our SageMaker workflow means our data scientists and customers spend less time wrangling data and more time building models that drive real enterprise value through Splunk.”

— Yash Sheth, Director of Engineering, Splunk Agent Observability

Chain capabilities from raw data to training

The value grows when you combine the capabilities. Some common patterns:

Build a golden evaluation dataset: Auto-label your raw data from a small seed set. High-confidence rows are accepted automatically, and low-confidence rows go to human reviewers. Their corrections improve the next labeling pass, resulting in a trusted, human-validated dataset to benchmark your models against.

Go from raw documents to a trained model in one workflow:

  • Generate data: Synthetic data generation creates task-specific examples grounded in your documents and seed data.
  • Transform it: Data transformation reshapes the data into the format your training technique expects, such as supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), or reinforcement learning (RL).
  • Validate it: Data quality evaluation checks the dataset for duplicates, leakage, and rule violations before you spend compute on training.
  • Train: Train with SageMaker AI model customization.

How it works

Consider a team preparing data to evaluate agentic customer support assistants. Its product guide says that a factory reset erases saved settings. The team wants to test whether the assistant preserves that warning when answering reset questions.

One pass through the preparation workflow looks like this:

  • Define the requirements: Supply the product guide as context and describe the questions and reference answers you need. Include the requirement that answers about a factory reset preserve the warning about saved settings. Review the specification produced with your coding agent.
  • Generate and inspect a sample: Generate a small batch and check the records against the guide. Review the generation and check the code. Confirm that the examples cover the intended questions and that the reference answers follow the source material.
  • Assess and review: Run a data quality assessment and inspect the record-level findings. Ask a subject matter expert to review ambiguous answers or disputed assessments. Use the results and annotations to request improvement recommendations.
  • Apply changes and repeat: Revise the specification if the requirements need clarification or transform the dataset to address issues such as duplicates. Generate additional examples where needed, then reassess the revised dataset before using it to evaluate the assistant.

This example workflow illustrates how the capabilities fit together.

Keep control of your preparation workflow and data

With the AI-ML skill, you describe the task in natural language while your coding agent helps build specifications, prepare code, and coordinate the data preparation steps. You can open those artifacts to see how the workflow is configured and make changes directly.

If you prefer to invoke the APIs yourself, use the Python SDK APIs to call individual capabilities from your own code. The SDK APIs take a specification as input, so we recommend creating it with the help of an agent. You can add quality assessment to an existing process, generate data for a new task, or combine several operations. You choose the preparation steps your project needs and how they fit into your model customization and evaluation processes.

AI Data Preparation runs with an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role that you control. Your source data, generated datasets, and labels stay in your own Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets, in the AWS Region you choose.

Get started today

The AI data preparation capabilities are generally available in the US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) Regions.

There are two ways to get started:

  • With your coding agent – Set up the data preparation skills in your supported notebook or IDE. Describe one training or evaluation task and review the resulting specification before generating a sample.
  • With Python – Use the SageMaker Python SDK directly to run individual data preparation capabilities from your own code. The SDK takes a specification as input, so we recommend creating your specifications with the AI-ML skill first, then using the SDK to run them in your workflow.

For more information, see the Amazon SageMaker AI documentation.

entries.title: Getting AI out of the demo and into businesses globally
entries.summary: Most enterprises have AI that works in a demo but stalls before production. AWS Forward Deployed Engineering closes that gap. AWS engineers embed with customer teams to take high-value workflows to production in 45-day sprints, leaving a foundation, workflows, and governance the customer owns.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Getting AI out of the demo and into businesses globally

AWS Forward Deployed Engineering is now available in 15 countries including U.S., Mexico, Brazil, Canada, Australia, Singapore, India, South Korea, Japan, UK, Germany, Netherlands, France, Sweden, and Saudi Arabia for commercial and public sector customers; and powered by dozens of built in production-ready accelerators.

Every enterprise I talk to has built something with AI that works. A prototype that reads a claim. An agent that resolves a card dispute. A model that answers a customer question in seconds.

The prototype works. The demo impresses stakeholders. Then the organization tries to put it into production, and the real problems begin. Production data is messier than the test set. Auditors want to know why the agent made each decision. Volume grows from a pilot group to the whole company. The rules that matter most turn out to live in people’s heads.

None of these are model problems. They’re business problems, and they decide whether AI ever pays off. The stretch from demo to production is the last mile, where most AI stalls. It’s also where our teams spend their time.

We launched AWS Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) in June to close that gap. Since then, we’ve worked through these problems with commercial and public sector customers in financial services, healthcare, sports, media, retail, and more. Here’s what we’ve learned, and how it shaped what we built.

The problem has three layers

Model providers, cloud providers, and consulting firms are all embedding engineers with customers. At AWS FDE, we measure success by what remains after our engineers leave: a foundation your team owns, workflows that keep learning, and governance you can trust.

Across customers, the hardest problems show up in three layers: the foundation, the workflows, and governance. Each one is harder than it looks, and each one builds on the one before it. That holds whether you’re starting fresh or building on existing systems. On a greenfield build, you can move fast, but there’s no foundation to stand on yet. On a brownfield system, agents must work within decades of data, rules, and integrations.

Layer one: A foundation that compounds

Before an agent can do useful work at scale, it needs a foundation: identity, security, context, governance, and operational controls. That foundation must be production-ready from day one and shared by every use case that follows. Context is often the biggest gap. Most customers have data spread across systems and no common ontology, the shared model of how the business works that agents need to reason over.

Without a shared foundation, the second pilot costs nearly as much as the first. Integrations get rebuilt, and lessons fail to carry forward. Most organizations reach a point where they stop and build the foundation first, so each new use case starts from what the last one built instead of from scratch. We call this the AI reset.

Samsung Life Insurance had four affiliates, each building its own AI point solutions from scratch. In 45 days, the FDE team built a governed agentic platform with a single control plane and compliance built in. New agents now deploy through registration and policy assignment instead of a rebuild.

Layer two: Automating workflows

Next is the work itself: High-volume, rule-heavy processes such as claims processing, know your customer (KYC) reviews, card disputes, loan origination, invoice reconciliation, permitting, and customer service. This is where AI can deliver immediate and measurable outcomes. The payoff is fast, but the knowledge that drives these processes rarely lives in a system. It lives with the people who do the work.

The hard part isn’t automation itself. It is uncovering the business rules behind each decision. When an invoice and a purchase order disagree, which record wins? When can an exception clear on its own, and when does it need a person? Experienced employees answer these questions from judgment, and that judgment is rarely written down.

Sometimes the knowledge is buried in the systems themselves.

Rio Tinto Iron Ore runs one of the world’s most complex mine-to-ship supply chains on a 30-year-old Oracle system. That system has more than 5,000 database tables and 140 applications. Mapping it had been a multi-month exercise. The FDE team built agents that mapped it in weeks, surfacing the dependencies that Rio Tinto’s teams could validate and build against.

Mapping what exists is only the start. The biggest opportunities emerge when organizations stop asking how AI can make existing work more efficient and start asking how it can change how work gets done.

Layer three: Governance that holds up as everything changes

Governance isn’t a phase of the project. It’s part of the architecture. As agents multiply, so do security risks, costs, and decisions you must explain. Every agent needs its own identity, permissions, and audit trail, separate from human identity. And because the models underneath are probabilistic, agents need monitoring that keeps their results predictable and auditable long after launch.

The system also must keep working as everything around it changes. Models drift, business rules shift, data formats change, and regulations tighten. New security issues appear, and code falls out of date. As newer models arrive, the instructions and tooling around them will change too. You need evaluations and guardrails that keep agents predictable where they must be and creative where they can be.

When governance comes at the end, it becomes the gate that stops production. When it’s built in from day one, it’s what lets your business move fast.

Marsh, a leading global professional services firm, needed agents that would hold up under its own audit standards. The FDE team built those controls in from the start, and the first use case reached production about two months after work began. Efficiency gains in the targeted areas have been as much as 70 percent, with some process steps moving from hours to seconds. Marsh has since expanded the work and keeps extending the system itself.

How we solve it: Speed, scale, and control

Our perspective comes from building and running these systems ourselves. AWS FDE pairs a small team of AWS engineers, scientists, and product managers with your engineers and a crew of specialized AI agents. Many of our FDEs come from the service teams that build Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Kiro, AWS Quick, and AWS Security Hub. They’ve built and run AI products at AWS scale, and they bring those engineering practices into your environment. Together, our teams take a high-value business problem to production in 45-day sprints, in your own AWS account. Customers shouldn’t need to choose between speed, scale, and control. FDE is built to deliver all three.

Speed – You might come to us with a broad goal or an ambiguous problem. We refine it with your business stakeholders, then build in your environment from day one, on your data and through your identity and security controls. We build in short cycles alongside the people who do the work. Each cycle puts real cases in front of them, and the unwritten rules come out as they react. We capture those rules in a living context, so the system keeps learning after we step back. Nothing gets rebuilt between prototype and production. You see working demos throughout, evaluations track progress against the outcomes you care about, and you have a production system within a quarter or less.

Scale – A point solution can move fast on one use case but leaves no foundation for the next five. Every FDE team works the same way, using the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), the method our own service teams use to take a broad problem to a working outcome. We deploy an opinionated AWS stack that reflects what we’ve learned building AI services, adapted to your environment: a living context of how your business works, a workbench where your engineers and agent crews build, a runtime on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and a control tower for governance, outcomes, cost, and agent performance. Accelerators for common tasks, such as document processing and customer sentiment analysis, handle the standard pieces, so each new workload can focus on what’s specific to your business. The opinionated AWS stack, context, and controls carry from one use case to the next.

Your context is what makes scaling possible. Say your first use case is a sales automation workflow. Because its context lives in your AWS account, the next use case, supply chain optimization, builds on it instead of starting over. Your context, tools, and AWS services all sit in one place, so each use case is faster to build than the last.

Control – You own what we build. Everything runs in your AWS account under your identity, network, and security controls. Your engineers work alongside ours from the first sprint, learning both the architecture and the delivery approach on a real business problem. They can then run and extend the solution long after the engagement ends. When we step back, your team runs the system from a control tower, a single view to govern, secure, and monitor every agent. We measure success by how much your team can build without us.

After the first or second project, we want you running AI software factories of your own. One financial services customer did exactly that with AI-DLC, with agents and engineers building together. Throughput rose 53%, and code reviews got 56% faster.

You also keep your choices open. Models are improving fast. When a better or more cost-effective model arrives, you can adopt it through Amazon Bedrock without rebuilding, so you control both capability and cost. You can also bring your own coding agents. Our opinionated AWS stack, adapted to your environment, connects to your systems through APIs, open standards, and connectors, and it works in hybrid environments. You keep the tools and partners you already use.

A flywheel where everyone gets better

Your team gets better. Your capability grows with every use case. The living context, the opinionated AWS stack, and your team’s skills carry forward, so the second use case doesn’t rebuild what the first one built.

AWS Services get better. Our engineers bring what they learn from customers back into the products. You build on the latest services, not a custom solution that falls out of date.

All of AWS works around you. Customer development engineering explores early ideas, FDE takes the hardest problems to production, AWS Professional Services and AWS Partners extend the work across your organization, and AWS Support keeps it running. You get the full depth of AWS behind your AI, and you stay in control of how you use it.

What’s new, and how to start

AWS FDE is now available in 15 countries to commercial and public sector customers, and it’s simpler to buy. Each 45-day sprint has a set price under the FDE Terms and is billed through your AWS account.

We work with customers wherever they are in their transformation. For customers starting out, we build a secure, governed foundation and the first workflows on it. For those ready to change how work gets done, we rebuild workflows such as claims processing and KYC reviews, along with the ones their customers use directly, like shopping and issue resolution. Agents then run the work. For those held back by legacy applications, we work with their engineers to build software factories they can reuse for each new workflow. For those already scaling in production, we keep systems secure with agents that find and fix issues, and we lower the cost per outcome.

If you’re ready to start, talk with your AWS account team. Bring an executive who owns the outcome and engineers ready to build alongside ours. We’ve learned where projects stall before they start, so our agents take on much of the setup, like access, data, and security checks. Work can begin within days. Then we agree together on what the first sprint will deliver and how we’ll measure success.

The gap between AI that works and AI that changes business outcomes is real. It is an engineering, operational, and organizational one, and our teams help customers close it every day. The organizations that succeed with AI won’t necessarily have the most advanced models. They’ll be the ones that build the foundation, workflows, and governance to scale AI across the business.

We’re still early, and we learn something new with every customer. The models will continue to evolve, and so will the tools around them. What should last is a foundation you own, workflows that keep learning, and governance you can trust. That’s what we mean by what remains after our engineers leave.

To get started, contact your AWS account team or learn more about AWS FDE.

entries.title: Build WhatsApp AI agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
entries.summary: SMART, an open-source Python SDK and Terraform stack, deploys the full WhatsApp channel layer to your AWS account with one command. Bring any agent that runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and SMART handles webhook ingestion, media, conversation memory, scheduling, and Meta message templates.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Build WhatsApp AI agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Across Latin America, India, and Southeast Asia, WhatsApp is one of the most widely used messaging applications. That makes it an obvious place to build an AI agent. For many end users, it is how they expect to interact with businesses. However, it is also a genuinely difficult surface to build for, even when your agent already runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

The agent is rarely the hard part. The integration is. Inbound messages arrive as deeply nested, type-dependent payloads that must be authenticated and normalized before your agent can read them. Media such as voice notes, images, and documents each require their own processing pipeline. Beyond message handling, you need conversation memory that survives sessions, durable schedules for reminders, and an authenticated path for external systems to trigger outbound messages. And anything you send more than 24 hours after the end user’s last message must use a pre-approved Meta message template.

Wiring that up means configuring more than 10 AWS services and learning a set of WhatsApp system behaviors that most teams discover only by hitting them. None of it is visible to a customer, but all of it has to work. Most teams either build it from scratch or hand the integration to a third-party service.

SMART (Social Messaging Agent Runtime Toolkit) is a third option: an open source Python SDK and Terraform stack that gives you the full channel layer. You provide an agent that runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, and SMART handles the rest. One command deploys the entire infrastructure to your AWS account.

Teams are already running on SMART with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Webmotors, originally scoped as a two-month engagement, compressed delivery to six weeks and moved their internal team into controlled production ahead of a full launch.

Whether you are starting from scratch or migrating an existing agent, you own the agent’s logic. You let SMART handle the channel.

The channel layer you don’t need to build

The following table compares what each concern costs to build yourself against what SMART provides.

ConcernBuilding it yourselfWith SMART
Webhook ingestionSignature verification, nested payloads, a dozen message typesHandled, so you receive a clean prompt
MediaDownload, transcribe, store, clean up, and upload outbound files before sendingFull lifecycle, both directions
Message templates and the 24-hour windowMeta approval flow, category rules, tracking which window each conversation is inDeclared in YAML, synced by CLI
Conversation memoryMulti-tier memory, session-break handlingAmazon Bedrock AgentCore memory, one function call
Scheduling and triggersAmazon EventBridge Scheduler wiring, authenticated ingress, routingBuilt in
InfrastructureMore than 10 AWS services stitched togetherOne 
terraform apply
Local developmentRedeploy and tunnel on every changeTest locally with the CLI without redeploying

The agentic layer

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. SMART builds on two of its main capabilities:

  • AgentCore runtime hosts and scales your agent without you managing infrastructure.
  • AgentCore memory persists conversation history across sessions and deployments, scoped to each phone number automatically.

Because AgentCore is framework-agnostic, so is SMART. Strands Agents gets memory wired automatically. LangGraph, Pydantic-AI, or another framework that gives you control over the conversation loop can integrate too. The SDK exposes the same memory and session hooks regardless of framework. You keep full control over the elements that differentiate your product: framework, model, prompt, and business logic.

The contract between SMART and your agent is deliberately small. Your agent receives the inbound message and returns text, optionally with rich message attachments. Everything else, session wiring, memory binding, delivery scheduling, is handled for you.

The following example is a complete 

agent.py
for a SMART project. The scaffolding command (
socialagent init
) creates the project structure and configuration around it. This file is where your agent logic lives.

The 

create_session_manager()
function binds the agent to AgentCore memory scoped to that phone number, so history survives across sessions and deployments for the memory retention period (7 days by default).

The 

socialagent_notify_context()
wrapper is the other pattern worth keeping. Tools sometimes need to send something while the agent is still working, such as a button list or a progress update. Sending it immediately corrupts the conversation history, and the user’s next message fails. The wrapper collects those messages instead, and they go out in order once the turn finishes. Your tools send messages normally and do not deal with the timing.

Architecture

The following diagram shows how an inbound message travels from WhatsApp to your agent and back, and where the shared infrastructure sits.

The SMART core stack is organized into distinct layers: message processing, an agent layer, and a service layer. AWS End User Messaging Social receives inbound WhatsApp messages and routes them to the processing layer. An AWS Lambda function handles the channel logic, while Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides the runtime, memory, and observability for the agent itself. Supporting services such as Amazon DynamoDB (optional, for per-user state), AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon CloudWatch, and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) supply state management, credentials, monitoring, and storage across the stack.

Inbound events arrive through Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS). On each event, the webhook Lambda function verifies the SNS message signature, normalizes the payload, and rate-limits each user (20 messages per minute by default, with the DynamoDB state table enabled). It then fires a read receipt and typing indicator, so the conversation feels alive before the model finishes. Voice notes go through Amazon Transcribe. Other media becomes a descriptor or goes to a hook you register if you want custom handling. When the agent throttles or fails, the user receives a readable message that you can customize, rather than silence.

Agents built on SMART interact directly with end users, so production deployments should include appropriate safeguards. The Terraform stack creates and configures an Amazon Bedrock Guardrails resource by default. With a single 

guardrail
variable in your environment configuration, you can use the stack’s default guardrail, bring your own, or opt out entirely. The controls that you apply are up to you. SMART makes sure the wiring is already in place.

After the message is ready, the webhook function passes it to AgentCore runtime. AgentCore memory maintains conversation context across sessions, and AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, traces every step for debugging and audit.

The webhook function sends the reply and messages your tools queued during the turn. A notification function handles sends outside a turn, such as proactive or scheduled messages. External systems trigger your event handlers by posting to an Amazon API Gateway endpoint protected by an API key and a Lambda authorizer. The event is published to Amazon SNS and the event Lambda runs your handler. Amazon EventBridge Scheduler handles time-based outreach, such as reminders and recurring check-ins. With message templates managed through AWS End User Messaging, you can send structured notifications outside the 24-hour WhatsApp session window.

A single 

socialagent deploy
provisions the following resources (it runs 
terraform apply
under the hood).
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime and AgentCore memory.
  • The webhook, notification, event, and scheduler Lambda functions, on Python 3.12, each with AWS X-Ray tracing and a dead-letter queue.
  • The Amazon SNS ingestion topic and the event API.
  • Amazon EventBridge Scheduler.
  • Amazon S3 buckets for media and audit trails.
  • Amazon CloudWatch dashboards and alarms.

The agent container image and the Lambda layer build in AWS CodeBuild during the apply. Docker isn’t required locally.

What you need

Before you deploy, confirm that you have the following.

  • AWS End User Messaging Social, with a WhatsApp Business Account (WABA) linked and a phone number registered. That account is the identity Meta issues to a business. For a step-by-step guide, see Getting started with AWS End User Messaging Social, which walks you through linking your WABA and registering a phone number.
  • An AWS account with AgentCore runtime and AgentCore memory available in your AWS Region, and model access enabled. This walkthrough uses Claude Haiku 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock by default. You can access many more foundation models (FMs) through Bedrock. See model support by Region.
  • Python 3.11 or later locally.
  • Terraform 1.7 or later, uv, and the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). The repository ships a starting-point AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy for the deployer role. See the infrastructure README for the full list of actions.

Note: This is sample code, for non-production usage. You should work with your security and legal teams to meet your organizational security, regulatory and compliance requirements before deployment.

Ship it

Start by cloning the repository and scaffolding a project.

The 

--blueprint
flag selects a project blueprint. Three blueprints ship, and 
minimal
is the default if you don’t pass an argument:
  • minimal
    : a bare-bones echo agent with no tools, skills, or message templates. Start here to build from scratch.
  • personal-assistant
    : a general-purpose assistant with conversation memory, per-user state, scheduling, skills, and rich/voice/image media tools, built on Strands. Start here for conversational, do-it-all agents.
  • appointment-scheduler
    : a booking agent that walks the user through a catalog of items and time slots, confirms the appointment, stores it as per-user state, and sends reminders. Start here for scheduling and booking flows.

You get a project with your 

agent.py
, 
socialagent.dev.yaml
(the project’s deployment configuration), handler stubs for the webhook, notification, event, and scheduler paths, and a vendored copy of 
socialagent_runtime/
. The personal assistant and appointment-scheduler blueprints also bring tools, skills, and a 
templates.yaml
for your message templates. 
minimal
ships none of those, so you add them as required.

Next, iterate locally, with no infrastructure at all.

The 

socialagent dev
command runs your real agent loop and real tools in a terminal read-eval-print loop (REPL), with AWS channel I/O stubbed. Memory becomes a local file-backed session, and state becomes a local JSON file shared across your dev sessions. Notifications print to the terminal, including buttons and list rows. One-shot schedules run immediately. Recurring ones are registered but do not fire. Tool calls appear inline. The reply arrives as one message, as on WhatsApp. The 
/event
and 
/schedule
commands exercise the handler paths. No deployment is involved, so you can test a change as soon as you save it.

Two caveats apply. The model call is real, so a blueprint other than 

minimal
needs AWS credentials and Amazon Bedrock access. The REPL also doesn’t simulate IAM or Meta’s template review. Testing through a deployed stack is highly recommended before you consider something done.

You can add capabilities as recipes. Each recipe is a plain Python function plus a markdown skill that teaches the agent when to use it.

Wiring the recipe to the agentic layer is the developer responsibility, which is what keeps recipes portable if you change agent frameworks.

When the behavior is right locally, deploy the stack.

One step Terraform cannot do for you. AWS End User Messaging Social needs to know where to deliver inbound messages. Point your WhatsApp Business Account at the Amazon SNS topic the stack created. That setting lives on the business account, not in the stack. Point the WABA’s event destination at the stack’s SNS topic using the admin console’s Bind action, or with 

aws socialmessaging put-whatsapp-business-account-event-destinations
from the CLI. Until it is linked, inbound messages go nowhere, and nothing errors.

When the project includes a 

templates.yaml
, the deploy step also syncs your message templates with Meta. If you need to sync templates independently, run 
uv run socialagent templates sync
, which reads the phone number ID and prefix from 
socialagent.dev.yaml
and the template definitions from 
templates.yaml
. A rejected template will fail the deploy, so fix the wording before retrying.

Meta sorts templates by purpose, and a transactional one has more permissive sending rules than a promotional one. Keep the wording plain. Emojis and marketing language are the usual reason a template gets reclassified as promotional. Running 

templates sync --force
re-registers every template, sending approved ones back through Meta review. A plain sync skips them. Leave approved templates alone unless you need to change their content.

Now you’re ready to message your WhatsApp number.

Operate it

Shipping one bot is a project. Operating a fleet of them is the part nobody budgets for, so you also get an optional administration console with its own Terraform root. Deploy it once. Each SMART stack that sets 

admin_registry_bucket
registers itself to a shared Amazon S3 registry on deploy, and the administration console discovers those stacks from there.

The console gives you fleet health at a glance, then per-bot depth. From a single stack view, you can do the following.

  • Read real conversations and reply by hand.
  • Inspect and cancel Amazon EventBridge schedules, and browse per-user state.
  • Restart an individual Lambda function or the runtime.
  • Review deployment history, recent errors, and Amazon CloudWatch logs.
  • Trigger test events.
  • Manage message templates with a WhatsApp-style rendering, and see a warning when Meta has reclassified one.

The console also owns the phone-number binding described earlier, so rebinding a number to a different stack is a UI action.

Sign-in runs through Amazon Cognito, with multi-factor authentication (MFA) required. Role-based permissions are then enforced on every API route. The console itself is served from Amazon CloudFront over a private Amazon S3 bucket.

The console runs on AWS services end to end. Every conversation stays within two providers: Meta and AWS. Model calls may be processed in other AWS Regions through Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference. See 

docs/data-flows.md
in the repository for details on inference routing, media processing, and service opt-out options.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, tear down the stacks in the following order.

Terraform will not remove three things. The media and audit S3 buckets block destroy while they hold objects, unless 

enable_force_destroy
is set. Templates registered with Meta persist. Your phone number registration is account-level and stays in place.

Get started

When building a WhatsApp AI product, the agent is where your differentiation lives. The channel integration is what eats your roadmap. SMART moves that boundary for you. Write a prompt, a few tools, and your business logic. In return you get webhook ingestion, media handling, conversation memory, scheduling, and template management. All backed by one-command infrastructure, a local development loop, and an administration console running in your own AWS account.

To go further, take the following next steps.

  • Get the code from the SMART repository on GitHub.
  • Set up your WhatsApp Business Account with AWS End User Messaging Social.
  • Start with 
    socialagent init
    and 
    socialagent dev
    , which need no AWS infrastructure.
  • Read the documentation in the repository for the areas this post summarized, including notifications, media handling, events and scheduling, per-user state, and message templates.
  • For further research, see the AgentCore documentation.

We would love to see what you build with it.

entries.title: Reason over time-series data with OpenTSLM on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
entries.summary: OpenTSLM, an open source family of time-series language models, is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. See how Nexthink and Aionic Labs apply it to proactive IT support, then deploy OpenTSLM to a real-time endpoint and fine-tune it on your own data with TimeNet and a SageMaker training job.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Reason over time-series data with OpenTSLM on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart

Across industries, decision-making starts with understanding what is changing and why. Industrial organizations collect data that informs decisions across their operations. This data helps prevent production stoppages, diagnose vehicle faults, explain drops in data-center performance, and adjust pricing as supply and demand shift. However, interpreting that data still requires specialist time, and collecting more data does not mean teams can act on it. General-purpose language models like Claude or ChatGPT can help analyze data. However, processing long histories across hundreds of operational metrics as text or images can consume large numbers of tokens, which increases cost.

To help organizations act on this data, Aionic Labs is developing temporal foundation models, including OpenTSLM, an open source family of time-series language models (TSLMs). These models interpret operational measurements, from equipment sensor data to supply and demand, alongside context such as maintenance records, market news, and an engineer’s observations. In doing so, TSLMs help systems recognize emerging problems in recent measurements. Experts can then ask follow-up questions to understand what changed and assess how to respond. TimeNet, the shared data infrastructure for time-series data, provides one format and API to find, build, and load the datasets used to train and evaluate these models. Together, they help organizations understand how their systems change and act before problems become costly.

OpenTSLM is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, so you can deploy the model in your own AWS environment. This post explores how Nexthink and Aionic Labs are bringing this capability to proactive IT assistance, then shows how to deploy OpenTSLM and adapt it to your own data using TimeNet.

A customer example: Proactive IT support at Nexthink

Nexthink and Aionic Labs are building toward a digital workplace where employees get help before they need to ask for it. At the center is Spark, Nexthink’s personal IT agent, enhanced with time-series language models that connect device telemetry and context to the problems employees experience. Spark turns that understanding into action: it checks the likely issue, guides the employee through an appropriate fix, and follows up on the result. Proactive assistance becomes part of keeping work moving.

The workflow combines recent device time-series, such as CPU activity, memory use, available disk space, application stability, and connectivity, with timestamped events and device and software context. The TSLM receives the numerical measurements alongside this text context and interprets how the signals change over the observation window.

The TSLM provides Spark with three outputs:

  • State summary: Explains the likely issue and the supporting signal patterns, connecting device behavior with the employee’s experience.
  • Recommended action: Specifies checks to confirm the issue and a practical action for Spark to offer the employee.
  • Expected outcome: Describes the intended improvement and how Spark checks the result.

Device telemetry and context support investigation of a range of issues, including slow performance under high CPU or memory load, recurring application freezes or crashes, and files that fail to synchronize. Resource usage, application events, storage measurements, and connection activity provide different pieces of evidence. Combined with device configuration and software versions, they give the TSLM a broader basis for explaining the employee’s experience and directing Spark’s next checks.

In the illustrative low-disk example in Figure 2, the TSLM connects declining free space, a rising disk queue, and more frequent application hangs with likely employee symptoms, such as a slow computer or difficulty saving files. Spark checks how much space is left and whether temporary files can be removed using an IT-approved cleanup. If the checks confirm that a cleanup is appropriate, Spark shows the employee what it proposes to remove and asks for confirmation. After the employee confirms, Spark runs the cleanup, checks the space now available, and asks whether the problem has improved. If the issue persists, Spark offers to pass the findings to IT support.

TSLMs understand how systems change and help people act on that understanding. For Spark, this means recognizing emerging IT problems and guiding employees toward a solution. The same approach brings time series intelligence to manufacturing, energy, and connected products, turning measurements and context into explanations and intelligent decisions.

Solution overview

The architecture in Figure 3 provides a reusable deployment pattern for time-series applications. SageMaker JumpStart supplies the model discovery and deployment path.

SageMaker JumpStart is a machine learning (ML) model hub that accelerates your ML journey. With SageMaker JumpStart, you can evaluate, compare, and deploy pretrained foundation models (FMs), including the newly available OpenTSLM model. As part of the AWS AI offerings, SageMaker JumpStart provides customizable ML solutions which you can deploy to Amazon SageMaker AI inference endpoints within your AWS infrastructure. It complements Amazon Bedrock, which offers serverless API foundation model inference along with features like customizations, knowledge bases, agents, and guardrails.

Key technical benefits of SageMaker AI and SageMaker JumpStart include:

  • Pre-built inference containers – AWS Deep Learning Containers with GPU acceleration, so you can serve the model without building your own image.
  • Automatic scaling endpoints – Managed infrastructure scales compute resources based on request volume and latency requirements.
  • Inference API – SageMaker real-time inference endpoints with standardized API calls, SDK, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) integration.
  • Integrated monitoring – Built-in metrics for throughput, latency, and resource utilization with an Amazon CloudWatch integration.
  • Enterprise security – Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) deployment with IAM access control and network isolation options.

The model in SageMaker JumpStart is OpenTSLM-Flamingo. It combines the Gemma 3 4B language model with a time-series encoder and cross-attention layers that let the language model attend to the encoded series. The model has 5.24 billion parameters in total, stored in bfloat16, so its weights take about 10.5 GB of GPU memory.

An application prepares numerical time series and text context, invokes the SageMaker endpoint, and receives the model’s response. The application can present that response to an expert or use it as input to another workflow.

This separation allows the application to control the observation window, select relevant signals, and validate the response before using it. It also makes the model independently adaptable: a new checkpoint can be evaluated against representative cases before the application switches to it.

In addition, we show a tutorial that fine-tunes a pretrained OpenTSLM checkpoint from Hugging Face using ARFBench data loaded through TimeNet. The notebook submits a SageMaker training job that loads ARFBench through TimeNet and fine-tunes the model. Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) stores the resulting model artifact, which is then deployed to a separate SageMaker real-time inference endpoint for evaluation.

Prerequisites

For the deployment walkthrough, use an AWS account with an Amazon SageMaker AI domain and a SageMaker AI execution role. The role must be able to create SageMaker models and endpoints in a supported Region, for example a role with the 

AmazonSageMakerFullAccess
managed policy. The quick setup for single users creates both. The managed policy grants broad permissions to get started. For production, use a policy that grants only the permissions you need, as described in Amazon SageMaker AI identity-based policy examples. OpenTSLM runs on a single GPU with at least 24 GB of memory and bfloat16 support, and we recommend 32 GB of host memory. The default instance type is 
ml.g6.2xlarge
(one NVIDIA L4 GPU with 24 GB of memory, 32 GB of host memory). In SageMaker JumpStart, OpenTSLM also supports 
ml.g6.4xlarge
, 
ml.g6.8xlarge
, 
ml.g5.2xlarge
, 
ml.g5.4xlarge
, 
ml.g5.8xlarge
, 
ml.g6e.xlarge
, and 
ml.g6e.2xlarge
. In the Service Quotas console, check your quota for “
ml.g6.2xlarge
for endpoint usage”, or for the instance type you choose. You need a quota of at least 1. If it’s lower, request an increase. See the OpenTSLM JumpStart model card for the model access requirements.

For fine-tuning, use JupyterLab in Amazon SageMaker Studio or a local Jupyter environment with AWS credentials configured to run the accompanying notebook, which submits the training job. The notebook uses the SageMaker default S3 bucket and an execution role. Fine-tuning runs on 

ml.g7e.2xlarge
, so also check your quota for “
ml.g7e.2xlarge
for training job usage”. Training runs on the job’s managed GPU instance. The notebook itself does not need a GPU. Obtain access to the selected Hugging Face checkpoint where required.

Deploy OpenTSLM with SageMaker JumpStart

To deploy OpenTSLM in SageMaker Studio, complete the following steps:

  • In SageMaker Studio, choose Models in the navigation pane, then JumpStart models.
  • Search for “OpenTSLM” and choose OpenTSLM-Flamingo Gemma 3 4B. The model page shows the model ID, the license, and the request and response format.
  • Choose Deploy.
  • On the Deploy model to endpoint form, review the Gemma Terms of Use under License agreement and select the checkbox to accept the end user license agreement (EULA). Keep the default instance type, 
    ml.g6.2xlarge
    , or choose another supported instance type. Then choose Deploy.
  • Wait until the endpoint status is InService. In our tests, this took about 6 minutes. Note the endpoint name, which starts with 
    jumpstart-dft-
    . You need it to send requests and to clean up.

You can also create the deployment from Python with the SageMaker Python SDK v3. The following example uses ModelBuilder. The model is gated: setting 

accept_eula=True
accepts its license, the Gemma Terms of Use. Review the terms before you deploy. The SDK prints a link to them when it builds the model.

Ask a question about a time series

The endpoint accepts a JSON request with one or more instances. Each instance holds a question, one or more numerical series, and optional context lines. Each series has its values, a name, and a short description of the signal, such as its unit and sampling interval. A series can hold up to 32,768 values. The endpoint scales each series to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1 and passes the original mean and standard deviation to the model as text, so the model receives both the shape and the scale of the signal. Use 

None
for a missing value. The model masks it.

Send the request with the SageMaker Runtime InvokeEndpoint API. Set ENDPOINT_NAME to match your deployment. The calling identity needs the 

sagemaker:InvokeEndpoint
permission. The following synthetic CPU example shows a request.

A request can hold up to four instances, each with 1 to 32 series, and the response contains one answer per instance in 

generated_text
. 
max_new_tokens
accepts values from 1 to 512. The model uses greedy decoding, so the same request typically returns the same answer. A real-time invocation must complete within 60 seconds, and the request body can be up to 6 MB. On 
ml.g6.2xlarge
, the model generates about 20 tokens per second. The endpoint processes the instances of a request in sequence, so response time grows with the number of instances and the length of the answers: an answer of 512 tokens takes about 30 seconds. To stay within 60 seconds, send several instances in one request only with short answers, for example with 
max_new_tokens
of 128. The 6 MB limit also bounds how much series data a request can carry. For long-running requests, you can use asynchronous inference.

You can send the same request with the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). Save the request as JSON, for example with 

json.dump(request, open("request.json", "w"))
, then run:

Choose an input window that preserves relevant events

OpenTSLM-Flamingo compresses the encoded time series into a fixed-size set of representations before the language model uses it. This bounds the representation passed to the language model, but it does not make the complete system unlimited in memory or guarantee that a brief event remains easy to identify in a very long recording.

Long-context research makes this distinction concrete. TS-Haystack evaluates event retrieval across recordings of different lengths and finds that the evaluated TSLM variants often lose accuracy as the history grows, especially when locating event start and end times. These results motivate testing the chosen checkpoint on the windows and questions used by your application.

Choose a window that contains the event and enough surrounding context to interpret it. For long recordings, compare overlapping windows. Preserve sampling resolution for brief events and align related channels in time. Include units, sampling interval, and the observation period in the text context. Validate both normal and abnormal examples at the intended lengths. The endpoint’s accepted payload size and the model’s useful analysis window are separate constraints.

Fine-tune OpenTSLM on ARFBench with SageMaker

Follow the accompanying fine-tuning notebook for the complete example, from preparing ARFBench data with TimeNet to launching a SageMaker training job and deploying the adapted model.

When should you fine-tune?

Start by testing the pretrained OpenTSLM model on representative examples from your application, and assess how well it answers your questions.

  • Use the pretrained model when its answers are correct and its explanations match the signals.
  • Improve the input when important information is missing, such as measurement units, sampling rate, system context, or the relevant time window.
  • Fine-tune the model when it consistently misses patterns specific to your domain or struggles with your task, even with sufficient context. Use representative signals paired with reviewed answers.

TimeNet provides a consistent way to load the data for training and evaluation. After fine-tuning, compare the adapted model with the original on examples that were not used for training.

Prepare fine-tuning data with TimeNet

ARFBench is a public benchmark of multiple-choice questions about anomalies in Datadog’s software-incident telemetry. We use ARFBench because its multiple-choice answers can be scored automatically, which makes the effect of fine-tuning measurable. The same workflow applies to tasks with open-ended answers, such as the summaries and recommended actions in the Nexthink example. TimeNet serves ARFBench as a versioned dataset: each question is stored with its answer options, its correct answer, and the metric signals. The training job loads ARFBench through TimeNet and the model checkpoint from Hugging Face.

Submit a SageMaker training job and deploy the fine-tuned model

A SageMaker training job runs the OpenTSLM training script on a GPU instance. The job fine-tunes the time-series encoder, the perceiver resampler, the cross-attention layers, and the language model’s token embeddings, and keeps the rest of the Gemma 3 language model frozen. The job saves the fine-tuned model to Amazon S3 in the layout of the Hugging Face model repository and writes the test accuracy before and after training to a 

metrics.json
file. If your SageMaker Studio domain has a default MLflow App, the job also logs the training and validation loss and the test accuracy to it, so you can compare runs in the MLflow UI. In our run on one 
ml.g7e.2xlarge
instance, accuracy on 135 held-out ARFBench questions rose from 5.0% to 45.9%. That is well above the 24.5% that random choice reaches on the full benchmark according to the ARFBench paper. Before fine-tuning, the model left most answers empty. Afterwards, it answered every question with one of the given options. ARFBench serves here as an example application: it shows how to adapt the model to a new task and answer format with a public dataset. The result is not a comparison with other models or an official ARFBench leaderboard result.

The following excerpt from the accompanying notebook starts the training job with 

ModelTrainer
. 
scripts/train.py
loads ARFBench, evaluates and fine-tunes the model, and saves it to 
FINETUNED_PREFIX
.

To deploy the fine-tuned model, create a new real-time endpoint on 

ml.g6.2xlarge
, or another instance type that the JumpStart model supports, with the same container image and environment variables as the JumpStart model, and the inference script that the accompanying notebook provides. Point its model data to the S3 location of the fine-tuned model files. The request format stays the same, so you can send it the requests from the previous section. The accompanying notebook contains the code.

Adapt the workflow to your domain

The same workflow can be adapted to other time-series tasks by pairing signal windows with relevant questions and reviewed answers. Potential examples include interpreting equipment behavior with maintenance context, explaining energy-consumption patterns with operating conditions, and describing activity from wearable measurements. The data, supervision, and evaluation should reflect the domain and the decision the application is intended to support.

Preserve the timing and meaning of the measurements during preparation, and separate training and evaluation data in a way that reflects deployment. For a predictive task, only information available at prediction time belongs in the input. Domain experts should assess whether an answer is grounded in the signals and useful for the intended workflow. For free-text answers, compare them with reviewed reference answers, for example through expert ratings or LLM-as-a-judge, where a language model scores each answer against a rubric.

Clean up

Deployed endpoints continue to incur charges until you delete them. When you finish, delete the endpoint, its endpoint configuration, and its model. If you deployed from SageMaker Studio, run the following commands instead of choosing Delete on the endpoint page, which deletes only the endpoint. The commands look up the configuration and model names from the endpoint name and delete all three. Set 

ENDPOINT_NAME
to the name of your endpoint, for example the default name that starts with 
jumpstart-dft-
for a Studio deployment:

Repeat these commands with the name of the fine-tuned endpoint. Stop the notebook application and remove tutorial-specific S3 data and artifacts that you do not intend to retain. The training job stops when it completes.

Conclusion

Time-series language models connect numerical measurements with the questions, context, and expertise people use to make decisions. Across manufacturing, energy, wearables, and digital infrastructure, they give people and applications a common way to interpret how systems change. The broader opportunity is to connect operational history with language, making past observations more useful in current decisions.

OpenTSLM is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, so you can deploy it to a real-time inference endpoint in your own AWS environment through SageMaker Studio or the SageMaker SDK. TimeNet and SageMaker training jobs provide a path to adapt the model to your domain’s signals and questions.

To get started, explore Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, follow the examples in the AWS Samples repository, and consult the OpenTSLM repository and TimeNet documentation. Start with the public ARFBench example, evaluate it on representative cases, then bring the signals, questions, and expertise from your own domain.
